value.text: For the second year in a row, Spanish River High School's football team won the 6A District 14 title. The Sharks are undefeated this season against district opponents and are 5-3 overall. Two of those Sharks are now preparing to swim into deeper waters: college football.You know them from Football Night in South Florida. Derek Goulbourne and Jayden Elder are frequent visitors to WPTV's weekly highlight show. That's because they produce plays that are must-watch football.WATCH BELOW: Spanish River stars headed to Army, FIUGoulbourne, a wide receiver, is committed to play college ball for Army next year."I really like the brotherhood that they have there. They all care deeply for each other and the coaches. They want to see the best from their players," Goulbourne said.The wide receiver has only been playing on the gridiron for four years."My freshman year, so as soon as I got into high school, I got the all-clear from my mom to start playing football, so I came out to practice, and that's when it began," Goulbourne said.He is now headed to West Point on a full scholarship."I'm very thankful for the opportunity," Goulbourne said.Goulbourne said he is eager to elevate his game at the next level."I'm definitely excited. The atmosphere is definitely something crazy. I mean, playing on Saturdays with the fans on TV, that's always amazing. But I think most importantly for me, I'm focused on elevating my game to the next level, always learning new things. That's a big goal for me to go in there and learn from the veterans so that hopefully I can make an impact," Goulbourne said.He said the bond with his teammates is what he'll miss most about high school."I'm definitely going to miss just like the energy here. You know, it's like you grew up with your teammates in high school. I think that it's really great the bond that we have on this team. So I'm definitely going to miss that for sure," Goulbourne said.Like Goubourne, teammate and wide receiver Jayden Elder is also college ball bound. But Elder's football journey began when he was young."I've been playing since I was 6 years old, so that was my first ever sport I played. Ever since I started playing, I never stopped, Elder said.Once this season wraps up, Elder too will miss playing as a Spanish River Shark."The brotherhood, learning, learning from my coaches, learning from my teammates, growing, growing a bond, a connection. That's really the main thing," Elder said.After years of putting in the work, Elder earned a roster spot and committed to Florida International University."It felt like a weight lifted off my chest for sure. All the hard work I put in finally felt like it was all coming together, so it felt good for sure," Elder said.He said he hopes to carry lessons from his coach into the next level."Keeping my composure for sure, keeping my head up, don't let my chin down. Stuff like that, just staying in the game, don't let nobody bring me down," Elder said.As for this season, Goubourne has his sights set high."Definitely hope that we make a good run in the playoffs. I don't want to end the season any earlier than the state championship. So that's definitely a big goal. And I know that my teammates definitely have the same goals," Goubourne said.Head coach Nick LaSala said Goulbourne is a versatile player, and even though he is a wide receiver, he can also be used in some cases like a tight end."He knows what everybody's doing on the field. He honestly might be the smartest player on our offense. He understands the run game. He obviously understands the pass game, explosive player, physical, just a well-rounded player," LaSala said.LaSala said Goulbourne's statistics on paper don't give the entire snapshot of his type of play between downs."I think last year, his numbers, they were good, but they probably weren't reflective of how important he was to our offense and all the stuff that he did," LaSala said.It's not a secret college recruitment can be a long and big process to take on, especially for high school student-athletes. But LaSala is there to do what he can, advocating for his players."I mean, you have the conversations with the college coaches in the offseason about all these different guys," LaSala said.Using film has been a big component of showcasing Goulbourne and Elder's skills on the field, LaSala said."Sometimes you just have to laugh at it because I get to see it on the practice field every day. But when they (college coaches) can't see it, all they can trust is the film. So there's definitely been a lot of that, and they've both done a good job of putting it on film," LaSala said.LaSala also shared the advice he has for Goulbourne and Elder as they take their football careers to the college level next year."If you just focus on being there and growing in the program and being invested in the people around you, it's going to work out for yourself because the rooms now in college, they change so quickly, which honestly, being in South Florida, they probably get a taste of that as well because South Florida invented the transfer portal," LaSala said.LaSala advises the players to simply take it all in, for all its worth, and to "just be where your feet are."The Spanish River Sharks round out the regular season with a game this Friday and will have their final home game on Nov.

Local food makers, artists and community organizations are getting a new waterfront showcase in Jupiter as Charlie & Joe's at Love Street launches a series of events designed to support local vendors and bring families together.The first Heart & Harvest market is scheduled for Saturday, Nov. at Love Street in Jupiter.Lucky Shuck Executive Chef John Daly told WPTV the event is focused on supporting the people who live and work in the community."It's all about supporting local, our local vendors, our local fishermen," Daly said during WPTV’s Shining A Light. "[It's a] good way to bring out the family, enjoy the outdoors, and come get a bite to eat."Schedule of Events• Saturday, Nov. to 2 p.m.: Taste of the Inlet – Heart & Harvest (green market)• Sunday, Nov. to 2 p.m.: Art in the Heart – Holiday Edition• Sunday, Dec. to 2 p.m.: Taste of the Inlet – Christmas Market at Love StreetAmong the vendors participating is Danielle Sarette of Seaside Sourdough.Sarette makes sourdough products from her home in Jupiter Farms and told WPTV that her children have become part of the family baking experience."My children love to come out with us to the vendors [to] the markets and be able to experience the joy that I have with [baking], and as well as baking with me," Sarette said. "(My kids) help me with the bread, the bagels, focaccia, everything that we make from scratch."Sarette also told WPTV that Seaside Sourdough recently launched a website, Seaside Sourdough.The market-style setting also provides a platform for The Arc of Palm Beach County's artisan program.Sean Stickley, the organization’s artisan program manager, showed WPTV artwork designed and assembled with adults participating in the program."Everything here is designed and put together with our adults, and they will get a commission check," Stickley said.The artwork provides another way for shoppers to support people in the community while looking for gifts ahead of the holidays.Stickley invited visitors to see the work in person, adding, "Hopefully you'll come out and see us and buy some stuff for Christmas or the holidays."Heart & Harvest is part of the larger "Events in the Heart" series at Charlie & Joe's at Love Street.According to event organizers, the series is built around four themes: Taste of the Inlet, Art in the Heart, Wellness in the Heart and Music in the Heart.The programming is intended to bring food, art, fitness and entertainment to the waterfront while giving local vendors and community groups opportunities to connect with visitors.That local connection is particularly timely heading into the holidays, when markets such as Heart & Harvest can introduce shoppers to small businesses and local artists while giving families another reason to spend time together outdoors.Heart & Harvest is scheduled for Saturday, Nov. at Charlie & Joe's at Love Street, 1116 Love St. in Jupiter.The broader Events in the Heart series is free and open to the community, although organizers say some individual activities and experiences may require advance registration and an additional fee.More information about upcoming events is available on the Love Street events page.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.What do you want me to Shine A Light on? What are you most proud of where you live? Email me at tawalker@wptv.com.

President Donald Trump is continuing a midterm campaign push less than a week until Election Day as Republicans try to maintain control of the House and Senate.Trump has crisscrossed the country holding near-daily rallies in the final month of the campaign in an effort to drive supporters to the polls.“We'll see what happens on Tuesday, but I think we've made a big impact,” Trump told reporters.The president sees his efforts “as the momentum shifter that Republicans have been waiting for,” according to a White House official, who said the president is fixated on winning both chambers of Congress.RELATED STORY | Trump rallies in South Carolina to boost GOP candidates ahead of midterms“I think that there is a real momentum shift based on just the overall aspect of seeing a quote-unquote doom and gloom midterm election to now seeing real excitement on the ground that is an undercurrent that people aren't necessarily talking about in the media per se,” the official said.Trump believes his rallies are helping boost Republican enthusiasm and support for candidates he is throwing his weight behind.“For whatever reason, presidents don't win, almost never, the midterms. And I think we've really turned it around. And, you know, I think the rallies have turned it, frankly, just to be honest. And every senator feels the same way,” Trump told reporters.Officials believe that’s coming to bear in returns.“I think that has direct application and direct response of what we are seeing in some of the early vote numbers,” the official added.There are "plenty of good signs in the returns from what we’ve seen,” an RNC official said, but noted still a lot of work to do.“The biggest thing I’m looking for in the data right now is what the electorate is shaping up to be. There’s different versions of that electorate that tell me a bit of a different story of what may happen in November,” the RNC official said.Republicans are looking for Trump to turn out his base of supporters.“POTUS will definitely help on the turnout end,” said the RNC official, who noted his base does not tend to be midterm voters. While the official acknowledged a larger hill to climb than democrats, they “always knew that would be the case.”Trump is imploring supporters to consider him on the ballot.“I’m asking you to pretend that I'm on the ballot. So when I'm on the ballot, when I'm on the ballot, I get 49.2% more votes. So when I'm not on the ballot, therefore, I don't get that, but I really am on the ballot if you think, because all of those tax cuts, all of the things that we've got and all of the victories that we've had with Venezuela, soon Iran, we'll close that one out too. All of the success we've had, you know, your state has the best numbers in history. And that's because of what we've done -- our economic policy,” Trump told supporters at an Ohio rally Wednesday.His campaign press comes as Americans express concerns over the economy and cost of living.At least three-quarters of respondents to an AP/NORC poll released earlier in October disapproved of the president’s handling of the economy and cost of living.The economy is the North Star, a senior administration official previously told Scripps News.On the campaign trail, the president has touted what he views as his administration’s accomplishments- things like private sector job growth, investments, foreign policy with Venezuela and Iran- and warned against democratic policies, announcing new economic- and energy-focused policy at many of his stops. That is expected to continue and that message generally won’t change, a senior administration official previously explained.“I mean the administration has a number of different wins to be able to sell in all of these different in all of these different states, and the cabinet, under the direction of the president, has done a good job of bringing real wins, bringing real tangible net positives to these different states,” said the White House official, who suggested this would continue to be discussed with “more to come.”However, the president’s approval rating has averaged below 40 percent in recent surveys and recent polling shows tight races in recent solidly red areas like Texas, Ohio and South Carolina where the president has made multiple stops.Trump has generally dismissed surveys, though, as do officials. A White House official contends there’s an oversaturation. “I do have a hard time believing whatever public polling is out there, because I just don't think it's accurate,” the official said. Another senior administration official previously contended the numbers are not as dire as thought if they go race by race and pointed to the Republicans' war chest.But some contend the president is not having the effect he’s touting.“I mean, his approval rating is in the toilet. I think there are some legitimate questions about the veracity of polling in some of these House races and Senate races, but it is not in dispute that America has grown tired of Donald Trump,” said a national Republican strategist.The strategist said the enthusiasm is with his base, “and that sounds like a lot of wishful thinking to me.”“We are going to see a tsunami in some areas and a heavy rainfall in others,” said the strategist. “Arizona, Nevada, some seats in California, I think, are going to be okay, but it seems like the Midwest and Texas and those areas are going to be potential tsunami.”There is a feeling the White House is bracing for a loss in both chambers, according to a former Trump campaign official. “It’s not a great feeling in the White House that this is happening,” the former official said, who contends Trump is frustrated he’s going to deep red areas.But Trump has expressed confidence about the midterms.Republicans “…are on offense in plenty of places where the narrative and the dems and these quote unquote republican strategists" would contend republicans are on the defense “and it’s false,” an RNC official said.In the homestretch, the strategy appears to generally stay the course.“In the home stretch to the most consequential midterm election, Republicans' strategy remains the same: expose Democrats' far-left agenda, flood the zone with resources, barnstorm the country, and drive our voters to the polls to defy midterm history,” stated RNC National Press Secretary Natalie Baldassarre.The outcome of the election could have a direct impact on the success or lack thereof of the President’s agenda.Trump has suggested that if Republicans do not maintain control of both chambers of Congress, he would rely on veto power.“If there was, as you call it, gridlock, what happens is I veto everything and then the Democrats come and they want to make a deal. So, we'll work with them,” Trump said.A former campaign official also pointed to the use of executive orders and interagency action.“They’ve done it before and it’s not gonna be a fun experience again,” said the former campaign official.The legislative affairs team “is probably planning for all scenarios with the expectation that we’re going to win both the House and the Senate back,” said a White House official.

Funeral arrangements have been announced for St. Lucie County Fire District Firefighter/Paramedic Austin Hodge, who died in the line of duty on Saturday.Hodge served the St. Lucie County community for more than nine years, according to the fire district.WATCH REPORT BELOW: St. Lucie County firefighter dies on duty"The St. Lucie County Fire District continues to mourn the loss of Firefighter/Paramedic Austin Hodge," the agency said in a statement. "His loss is deeply felt by his family, friends, fellow firefighters, and the many lives he touched throughout his years of service."A public viewing will be held Friday, Nov. at River of Life Fellowship Church, located at 3950 Juanita Avenue in Fort Pierce.A memorial service will follow Saturday, Nov. at Christ Fellowship Church, located at 10250 SW Village Parkway in Port St. Lucie.The fire district said the arrangements were made in coordination with Hodge's family and Stone Brothers Funeral Home.Officials thanked the community for the support shown to Hodge's family and members of the fire district following his death."We remain grateful for the outpouring of love and support extended to Austin's family and our Fire District family during this difficult time," the agency said.The release did not provide additional details about the circumstances surrounding Hodge's death.

Palm Beach County sheriff's deputies discharged their firearms following a hours-long negotiation with an armed person who was threatening suicide Wednesday night, according to the Palm Beach County Sheriff’s Office.WATCH: Sheriff Ric Bradshaw gives update on fatal shootingDeputies responded shortly before 10 p.m. Wednesday to Sandalfoot Square at 23066 State Road 7 near Boca Raton, after receiving a call from relatives of an armed man who "was very suicidal," Sheriff Ric Bradshaw said Thursday during a press conference.Deputies arrived to find the 30-year-old Army veteran sitting on the ground in front of the open driver's side door of his car, leaning back against the running board, with a gun in his left hand. He repeatedly put the weapon to his head during the standoff, the sheriff said."He said, 'I want to die. I want to kill myself,'" Bradshaw said. He put it to his head several times." According to PBSO, deputies spent several hours negotiating with the man, who suffered from PTSD and had been drinking, from 9:55 p.m. before the incident resulted in deputies firing their weapons."They talked to this guy a long, long time trying to talk him down. Even one of our guys who's a vet kind of connected with him a little bit and told them, 'Hey, you know, we're going to get you the help you need,'" Bradshaw said. "But it was pretty obvious he's decided that this was the end of the day for him, and then that's when he made his move and they had to do what they had to do." The sheriff said the man became agitated and began to stand up with the gun in a "ready position." Deputies, perceiving a threat, opened fire."I would characterize that the gun was in a ready position. Yes, that's what I would characterize it as. He's obviously making an assertive, aggressive mood coming off the ground with the gun in the ready position," Bradshaw said.Deputies immediately attempted CPR and called fire rescue to the scene, but the man died, the sheriff said.The gun recovered appeared to be a 9mm handgun with an extended magazine, which holds more rounds than a standard magazine, the sheriff said. When asked whether the man pointed the gun at deputies or fired at them, Bradshaw said the man did not shoot back and that deputies did not wait for him to do so."No, no, they didn't give him that opportunity," he said. "See, that's the idea, when people present to you that you're going to be in jeopardy, you don't have to wait till they shoot at you. That's not smart."The sheriff said he could not yet confirm the origin of what appeared to be bullet holes in one of the agency's cruisers that was towed from the scene, saying he had not yet spoken with investigators about it.The Florida Department of Law Enforcement is investigating the shooting. The deputies involved are on paid administrative leave as the investigation continues, the sheriff said.

A report alleging efforts to recruit a candidate who shares the same name as Alaska Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan has injected fresh controversy into one of the nation's most closely watched U.S. Senate races, where control of the chamber could ultimately be at stake.The controversy centers on a New York Times report detailing efforts by Democrats to encourage another Dan Sullivan, a retired teacher with no major political profile, to enter the race. The move would have placed two candidates named Dan Sullivan on the ballot: the incumbent Republican senator and the retired educator.The report has prompted Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy to order a criminal investigation into the matter, raising questions about whether any state laws may have been violated. Legal experts, however, have expressed skepticism about whether the reported conduct amounts to a crime.Democratic candidate Mary Peltola's campaign has denied involvement. In a statement, the campaign said it had "no involvement in either Sullivan campaign."The allegations have become a flashpoint because of Alaska's importance in the battle for Senate control. Political analysts rank the race among the nation's top tier of competitive contests, and even a small shift in votes could prove consequential.Alaska's election system relies heavily on mail voting, with a significant portion of ballots already cast. As voters review their ballots, some Republicans worry that the presence of two candidates with the same name could create confusion and potentially siphon votes from the incumbent senator.While political observers generally expect Republican voters to support the sitting senator, critics argue that even a small number of mistaken votes could influence the outcome if the race is decided by a narrow margin.The controversy gained additional national attention after former President Donald Trump accused Democrats of wrongdoing and called for severe consequences."They said they didn't do it, and we caught them cold," Trump told reporters, adding that Peltola should resign and that those involved should face prosecution.No criminal charges have been filed, and it remains unclear whether investigators will identify any violations of law.RELATED STORY | Report: Peltola campaign linked to effort to recruit second Dan Sullivan in Alaska Senate raceRepublican Sen. Lisa Murkowski of Alaska also weighed in on the controversy. Murkowski, a prominent figure in Alaska politics who has at times broken with her party and previously endorsed Peltola in other races, criticized what she described as "ballot stacking."In a statement posted on social media, Murkowski said, "Ballot stacking should have no place in our electoral process." She also accused Peltola's campaign of engaging in "a pattern of lies and cover-ups and a culture of deception."The dispute highlights the high stakes surrounding the Alaska race. Because the Senate majority could hinge on the outcome, both parties are closely scrutinizing developments that might influence voter behavior.Political analysts say the controversy's long-term impact may depend on the election results. If Sullivan wins, the issue could quickly fade from public attention. If Peltola prevails in a close contest, however, Republicans could pursue extended legal and political challenges while continuing to scrutinize how the second Dan Sullivan's candidacy emerged.RELATED STORY | Trump says he ordered the Justice Department's lawsuit over Alaska's US Senate raceFor now, the allegations have added another layer of uncertainty to an already competitive race, underscoring how even unconventional campaign tactics can become major issues when control of the Senate hangs in the balance.

President Donald Trump is rallying in South Carolina for a second time this month in the final days of the midterm campaign.Trump will appear in Rock Hill, which is south of Charlotte and near the North Carolina border, to shore up support for Sen. Darline Graham in South Carolina, Michael Whatley in North Carolina and other republican candidates.“She’s doing well,” Trump told reporters Wednesday. “She’s up.”In the historically red state, the race between Graham and Democratic nominee Annie Andrews has shown to be more competitive. A recent NYT/Sienna poll found the race was a toss-up at around 48% each, though other recent surveys have shown Graham with an advantage.RELATED STORY | Trump fires back after Obama compares White House to Cheesecake FactoryTrump has spent both time and money supporting Graham in the general election and Republican primary following the death of her brother, the late Sen. Darline Graham has expressed support for Trump, though some difference emerged following the President’s decision to waive sanctions against Russia in legislation that was championed by her brother.“This is a state that President Trump has carried three times. This is a state that supports his agenda, supports the president and his accomplishments from tax cuts to border security to safe communities, backing the blue, made in America investment boom,” said an RNC official, pointing to a “stark contrast on the ballot between, you know, a common sense conservative Darlene Graham and a really radical Democrat Annie Andrews.”The president believes his rallies are helping boost Republican enthusiasm and support for candidates he’s backing, as he implores supporters to turn out.“Republicans are taking nothing for granted. We are getting out the vote every single day in every single state to make sure that the president is able to maintain the Republican majorities in the House and the Senate,” the official said. “There is no one that turns out voters like President Trump. And to be able to barnstorm the country like this really shows the difference in the energy between, or the difference in the energy that we're seeing on the Republican side versus on the Democrat side.”RELATED STORY | Trump makes last-minute push to keep Texas in Republican hands with third tripHowever, Democrats believe Andrews is in a strong position in the homestretch.”Annie Andrews is running an incredibly formidable campaign against Darline Graham, a weak candidate whose campaign has been defined by embarrassing gaffes and full-throated support for the policies spiking the cost of gas, groceries, and health care for South Carolinians,” said Monica Robinson, DSCC Spokesperson. “Annie has made this race competitive and is in a strong position heading into the final stretch, while the GOP scrambles to prop up struggling, second-rate candidates as their disastrous agenda continues raising costs and hurting voters across the map.”Meanwhile in North Carolina, former RNC chair Michael Whatley has trailed in polling against former governor Roy Cooper for the state’s U.S. Republicans acknowledge tight races in the state, according to a Republican official, but believe the president and vice president’s visits to the state are helping boost turnout.Trump is expected to hold more rallies in Florida, Kansas and Iowa in the days ahead.

Lucie man was arrested on charges alleging he threatened to file lawsuits and ethics complaints against State Rep. Meg Weinberger unless she publicly apologized and backed his push for government audits, according to a Palm Beach County Sheriff's Offic e probable cause affidavit. Anthony Pizzarelli, 50, was booked Oct. He faces charges of extortion, using a two-way communication device to facilitate a felony, and harassing an elected official, according to the affidavit. The charges are allegations; Pizzarelli is presumed innocent unless proven guilty. Investigators say Pizzarelli emailed Weinberger on Feb. 9 and offered to leave her out of lawsuits and ethics complaints he said he planned to file if she issued a swift public apology. He also proposed wording for the apology. In an April 6 email, he allegedly renewed the threat, writing that he did not plan to name her in the complaints but that can change, and urged her to help with his audit campaign. According to the affidavit, Pizzarelli transmitted a voice memo May 18th, 2026, directly to Weinberger's personal cell phone in which he stated, among other things: "I'm an angry person, so I'm not being nice," "I'm doing the lawsuits," and "you don't know what I can do." The affidavit says Pizzarelli wanted Weinberger to support audits of Palm Beach and St. Lucie counties and pursue investigations into government contracting. Weinberger told investigators she had never met him, did not represent him and had no authority over St. She said she viewed the messages as threats and feared for her safety and her family’s, according to the affidavit. Pizzarelli told investigators he viewed his communications as good faith notices and denied using them to leverage Weinberger. He said he was seeking an apology over an incident in which she had been copied on an email, and was trying to get her support for his complaints. He had not filed a lawsuit or ethics complaint against her at the time of his interview, the affidavit says. See also: Florida woman convicted in $8.6 million Medicare fraud scheme The affidavit says the investigation found probable cause for the charges after reviewing emails, a May voice message and evidence from electronic devices. Prior accusation of threats In 2025, Pizzarelli was accused of sending threatening emails to St. Lucie County commissioners. Deputies say the communications escalated in tone and content, which raised concern among officials. In the emails he sent, he allegedly using threatening language that included being "ruthless" and making allusions to "murder charges where applicable." Pizzarelli was arrested and booked on counts of intimidation - sending written threats to kill or injure. In the current affidavit, Pizzarelli told investigators that all charges from the 2025 case had been dropped. Weinberger, running for reelection, faced intimidation in 2024 Weinberger, a first-term Republican, represents Florida House District 94 in Palm Beach County, according to the Florida House. Weinberger’s campaign faced a separate voter intimidation case during the 2024 election. Nicholas Farley was arrested after a campaign volunteer said he yelled antisemitic slurs at her and drove threateningly near early voters outside the Acreage Branch Library. Farley told detectives that seeing Weinberger campaign posters triggered his remarks. The case involved Farley, not Pizzarelli. Absolutely it’s very scary we’re dealing with this. It’s just no way to live and maybe he opens his eyes and realize that we’re just all people doesn’t matter your religion or skin color, Weinberger said at the time. Weinberger is seeking reelection on Tuesday. She faces Democrat Elizabeth Holmes and Doug Barrow (no party affiliation). Related: Early voting ends this weekend across Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast She was behind the bill that pushed to rename PBIA in honor of President Donald Trump. House District 94 is entirely within Palm Beach County. It stretches from the western Glades communities of Belle Glade, Pahokee and South Bay through areas such as Westlake, Loxahatchee Groves, The Acreage and Jupiter Farms, and includes parts of several eastern communities, including West Palm Beach, Palm Beach Gardens, Jupiter and Royal Palm Beach.

Nearly eight years after WPTV first investigated concerns about a possible cluster of glioblastoma cases in St. Lucie County, health officials have reviewed the numbers again.The latest findings show the number of cases remains in line with what would be expected based on the county's population, but families who lost loved ones to the deadly brain cancer say important questions remain unanswered.WATCH THE REPORT BELOW: The latest review by the Florida Department of Health follows years of WPTV reporting into concerns raised by patients and families who discovered they lived near others diagnosed with the same aggressive form of brain cancer.While health officials say the data does not show a statistically significant increase in cases, the review does not examine whether patients were concentrated on particular streets or in specific neighborhoods.For families who have spent years searching for answers, that distinction matters.READ THE FULL STATE REPORT BELOW: A young man's death helped spark an investigationFor Deb Johnston, the loss of her son, Lenny Schelin Jr., is still painful."It's been eight years since Lenny passed," she said.Lenny was just 33 years old when he died from glioblastoma, one of the most aggressive forms of brain cancer.He was healthy, active and loved fishing. He survived just 17 months after his diagnosis."Everybody loved Lenny. He just had this charm about him," his mother recalled.Lenny's story was among the first that helped WPTV uncover concerns about glioblastoma cases in St. Lucie County.Other patients included Mark Cunningham, who was also in his 30s, and Kyle Vericella, who was just 18.After WPTV anchor Meghan McRoberts uncovered the local cases, dozens of additional patients and family members contacted her with their stories.Area doctors and neurosurgeons also expressed concerns.Glioblastoma is most commonly diagnosed in older adults, making the younger ages of some patients particularly troubling to their families.But it wasn't just their ages that raised questions.As patients began connecting with one another, WPTV mapped where they lived beginning in 2018.Some lived within blocks of one another. Others lived on the same street. In one case, unrelated patients had lived in the same home.The reporting drew attention from lawmakers, environmental advocate Erin Brockovich and the Florida Department of Health.What did the original 2019 investigation find?The concerns prompted health officials to examine glioblastoma cases in St. Lucie County."You brought it to my attention. It was alarming; it was nerve-wracking," Clint Sperber, administrator for the Florida Department of Health in St. Lucie County, told WPTV's Meghan McRoberts.Sperber said the concerns led to a request for assistance from Florida's cancer registry."I asked for assistance from our cancer registry through our leadership, my boss," he said. "And we were able to help collect a lot of information."That information was compiled into a report released in 2019.Despite concerns about the number of patients diagnosed with glioblastoma, the report did not find a statistically significant increase in cases that would warrant a more intensive investigation.Health officials also reviewed existing environmental monitoring information, including public water utility data and radiation monitoring records associated with the area's power plant.Sperber pointed to ongoing environmental monitoring as part of the state's assessment."There is water testing, there is vegetation testing, they look at watermelon, milk, fish, soil, they would know if there is any release of radiation," Sperber said.The findings were disappointing for families who had hoped the investigation would uncover an explanation."I was like deflated because we worked so hard," Johnston said.What does the latest glioblastoma review show?Seven years after the original report, health officials have taken another look at glioblastoma cases in St. Lucie County.Their conclusion remains largely unchanged."The conclusion that was found in 2019 is the same one we have today," Sperber told WPTV. "We are seeing the same ratio, the same expected number of cases that we would expect statewide for our county."According to Sperber, a county with approximately 400,000 residents would be expected to see about 14 to 15 new glioblastoma diagnoses each year.The report also shows that from 2019 to 2023, there were 95 cases of glioblastoma, just three cases more than the 92 expected.Health officials say the latest review does not identify an unusual increase in glioblastoma cases compared with statewide expectations.Unlike the 2019 report, however, the latest review does not break down cases by age or sex.Officials say there are too few cases to make those comparisons statistically reliable.The review also considered existing water and radiation monitoring records without identifying new concerns.What questions remain?Although the latest review did not find an unusual increase in glioblastoma cases countywide, it does not settle every question raised by patients and their families.Sperber acknowledged the analysis does not closely examine whether patients lived near one another on particular streets or within specific neighborhoods.That means the review's broader findings do not necessarily address the geographic patterns that originally concerned families, determining what causes glioblastoma is also challenging.Sperber pointed to recent research by the International Journal of Molecular Sciences identifying nearly a dozen potential factors associated with the disease, making it difficult to identify a single environmental source."I wish there was an answer," Sperber said. "I wish there was a smoking gun that says okay here is the reason, the cause, the source for glioblastoma."As St. Lucie County's population continues to grow, health officials expect the total number of diagnoses to rise as well.But for families who lost loved ones, the question remains whether the countywide numbers tell the entire story.A mother's call for a closer look at her hometownFor Johnston, hearing that the state's findings have not changed was difficult."I was deflated when you told me that. A Delray Beach homeowner says a new roof and a new insurance company resulted in a new worry over money."My finances are very limited," says 83-year-old Doris Fiorenza.WATCH REPORT BELOW: "I only have Social Security, I'm low income, and with all these bills I'm getting hit with, I'm going to run out of money."Doris says that after she got a new roof on her villa, which cost $14,000, she was dropped by Citizens Insurance.She found a private insurer, but her premium of around $3,300 is far higher than the $1,800 she was paying to Citizens.Part of the problem was a $900 surcharge on her policy for a lapse in coverage between her Citizens policy and her new policy.It's a mistake homeowners need to know can be costly.Homeowners also need to know that improvements like a new roof do trigger insurance discounts."It's happening to a lot of people," says Robert Norberg of Arden Insurance in Lantana."That's what we tell everybody: when you get upgrades that get you credits, always, always turn them into your current company, make sure those get processed."Norberg also says homeowners are saving money by shopping around to find better premiums."A lot of our clients are able to get either a better rate," he says. "It's very competitive; rates are changing a lot, they all seem to be going down, and the other companies are getting really aggressive."

Boynton Beach city leaders are considering potential changes to the city's parking ordinance after residents raised concerns about limited parking options and challenges enforcing the rules in different neighborhoods.The ordinance, which took effect in February, restricts parking on public streets, swales and sidewalks. Violations can result in a $25 fine.WATCH REPORT BELOW:Residents hosting parties, family gatherings or open houses can temporarily allow yard parking for up to 12 hours within 24 hours, provided vehicles do not obstruct traffic.While some residents say the rules have improved neighborhood conditions, others argue they do not account for differences in neighborhood layouts and homeowners association (HOA) restrictions.At a recent commission meeting, Commissioner Aimee Kelley raised concerns about residents in District Four who have limited options for parking on their own property."We're running into an issue where what might work in other areas of the city are not working in District Four," Kelley said.Kelley explained that some HOAs prohibit residents from parking in swales or expanding their driveways, leaving public streets as their only practical parking option."They're limited by their HOA on how they can enhance or modify their driveways, so they can't make more parking," Kelley said.District Two faces a different set of challenges, including narrow streets, small lots and limited driveway space. City officials said enforcement in that district remains on hold while traffic-engineering plans are developed.Boynton Beach Police Chief Joseph DeGiulio also questioned whether the ordinance's existing exceptions can be enforced consistently.DeGiulio said monitoring whether a vehicle has exceeded the 12-hour parking allowance is difficult for enforcement personnel."The 12-hour parking, that's another thing; we can't enforce that. We can't sit in front of a car for 12 hours," DeGiulio said.One potential solution discussed at the meeting is establishing specific overnight parking restrictions. Steve Burdelski suggested prohibiting street parking between midnight and 6 a.m. as one option for the commission to consider.Officials also discussed identifying specific streets or areas that may need exceptions, as well as installing no-parking signs on roads where parked vehicles could prevent emergency responders from getting through.However, some city leaders emphasized that the current ordinance has helped address longstanding parking and accessibility concerns in certain neighborhoods.Commissioner Thomas Turkin said the changes have made a noticeable difference in his neighborhood."Our neighborhood has been cleaned up dramatically. People can navigate," Turkin said.City leaders agreed that any changes should address the different needs of neighborhoods without reversing improvements to public safety, sidewalk access and emergency vehicle clearance.No changes have been finalized. City staff will work with commissioners and the mayor to develop potential amendments and return with options for further discussion in December.

Developer Mattamy Homes is transferring 125 acres to Martin County in support of restoring the St. Lucie River.The developer said the parcel was donated from the northern section of the Newfield development to the Comprehensive Everglades Restoration Plan, a federal plan to restore, protect, and preserve South Florida's water resources.WATCH REPORT BELOW: James Fitzgerald, vice president of community development for Mattamy Homes Southeast Florida Division, said the land will have the capacity to host large amounts of muck that will need to be dredged out of the St. Lucie River to improve water quality. The affidavit says Pizzarelli wanted Weinberger to support audits of Palm Beach and St. Lucie counties and pursue investigations into government contracting. The family of Kalibe Combs, a 23-year-old Road Ranger killed while working at an Interstate 95 crash scene near Lantana Road, is remembering the young father as a loving caretaker while calling for changes they hope could protect other roadside workers.Combs was struck early Sunday on northbound I-95 near Lantana Road while working at an existing crash investigation, according to the Florida Highway Patrol. Investigators said an 18-year-old driver entered a closed lane, struck Combs and then collided with a marked FHP cruiser. Combs died at the scene.WATCH: Family remembers Road Ranger killed on I-95 as loving father, caretakerCombs leaves behind his fiancée, Siarah Rodriguez, and their 3-month-old daughter, Kiara, according to his family and a fundraiser established to support them."He brought a lot of light. So losing him, we're losing a lot of light," his mother, Aretta Combs, told WPTV.'He was a caretaker'Combs' family told WPTV he was funny, kind and hardworking. His mother said his commitment to his family was at the center of the life he was building."He was a caretaker. He lost his life trying to provide for his family, trying to take care of his family," Aretta Combs said. "So what's more heartbreaking is that something like this can happen and change the lives of so many people."The family says Combs had worked as a Road Ranger and took pride in helping people while providing for his family.His death came at a moment of major change for the young family. The fundraiser says Combs and Siarah Rodriguez were recently engaged and raising their infant daughter, Kiara Rodriguez-Combs."Very loving, always wanted to take care of me and very excited about the baby," Rodriguez told WPTV.For Combs' family, the loss is still difficult to comprehend."I think we are all in shock," Aretta Combs said.When WPTV's Zitlali Solache asked whether it felt real, she replied, "No, it doesn't feel real."Family calls for greater roadside safetyAs the Florida Highway Patrol investigates the crash, Combs' family says they want his death to lead to changes that could make roadside work safer."I want to see safety. I want to see change," Aretta Combs told WPTV.She said no change can alter what happened to her son, but she hopes action could prevent another family from experiencing the same loss."I feel like there are changes that could be made," she said. "It's not gonna change our outcome, but it can change the other lives of other people."FHP previously said the crash happened around 2:07 a.m. on northbound I-95 near Lantana Road. A marked FHP Dodge Charger was positioned across two lanes with its emergency lights activated for a lane closure when investigators said the Mercedes entered the closed lane. The 18-year-old driver suffered non-incapacitating injuries and was taken to a hospital, according to FHP.Fundraiser established for Combs' familyA GoFundMe fundraiser, "Carry Forward Kalibe's Future", has been established for Rodriguez and their daughter. The fundraiser says donations are intended to help with their everyday needs, provide stability for Kiara's future and help the family honor Combs' memory.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Lucie County sheriff's deputy has been charged with DUI following a March 1 crash in Vero Beach that left a woman seriously injured and her son hospitalized. The crash happened at the intersection of Beachland Boulevard and A1A in Vero Beach. Investigators said Tyler Horstman, an off-duty St. Lucie County sheriff's detective, was driving an unmarked agency pickup truck when it collided with an SUV carrying a woman and her son. According to investigators, the SUV's driver ran a red light, while Horstman had a green light. All three individuals involved in the crash were hospitalized. The child was later released, but the woman suffered a traumatic brain injury, according to the affidavit. Police said the crash could have been fatal. "Given the nature of the vehicles at a decent rate of speed, I mean, I don't want to say it worked out in its best. I mean, obviously injuries were still sustained, possibly long-lasting injuries, but at the end of the day, it's very feasible that a fatality could have occurred," Lt. Investigators determined that Horstman's blood alcohol level was above the legal limit. According to the affidavit, Horstman stated during his assessment that he had "a few beers" earlier in the evening. Deep Dive: WPBF 25 News Investigates Police also said the truck was traveling about 64 mph in a 35-mph zone just before the crash. Horstman turned himself in on Monday. Police explained that the investigation took several months to complete. "It was a matter of investigators going through search warrants, subpoenas, and obtaining all different records," Kerensky said. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro, Horstman subsequently turned himself in to the Indian River County Jail and was placed on unpaid administrative leave in accordance with agency policy. "The men and women of this agency work every day to earn the trust of our community, and we will continue to hold ourselves to the standards that trust requires." With less than a week until Election Day, the race for Palm Beach County Commission District 6 is putting some of western Palm Beach County's biggest issues directly before voters. Republican incumbent Sara Baxter and Democratic challenger Katherine Waldron spoke separately with WPTV reporter Michael Hoffman about affordability, development and traffic, transparency and the debate over AI data centers.WATCH REPORT BELOW: Baxter, Waldron make their case to voters The two candidates emerged from their respective primaries and will face each other in the general election. Baxter is seeking another term representing District 6, while Waldron is looking to bring her previous experience at the Port of Palm Beach and in the Florida House to the County Commission.Hoffman has been following the District 6 contest for months. As the race enters its final stretch, he pressed both candidates on how their experience would shape their approach to some of the district's most contentious issues.Baxter is the Republican incumbent. Her time representing District 6 is her first elected political office. She has also been endorsed by President Donald Trump."We're putting in a lot of hard work," Baxter told WPTV reporter Michael Hoffman.Waldron, a Democrat, previously served as a Port of Palm Beach commissioner before serving one term as a state representative."We're out there every day," Waldron told Hoffman.That difference in experience has become part of the choice before voters. Baxter points to her record on the County Commission, while Waldron points to her experience in multiple elected offices.Hoffman asked both candidates about affordability, traffic and development, issues affecting residents across District 6.Waldron argued that transparency has been lacking and said she has heard from residents who don't believe their concerns are being heard."My general sense when I've been out there talking to voters in my district and beyond is that they feel like they're not being heard. They feel like there's not transparency," Waldron told Hoffman.She also questioned whether enough is being done to mitigate the effects of development on surrounding communities."They're not really looking into or trying to mitigate the impact that it will have on the constituents, on schools, on traffic, on quality of life," Waldron said.Baxter pointed voters to her record on the commission, telling Hoffman she has tried to fight for residents while navigating competing opinions within the district."I have always tried to do what's best for the residents and fight for them. And sometimes I have residents on different sides of issues," Baxter said.Baxter said residents can look at her previous votes and commission meetings when deciding whether she has effectively represented them."I think, in my seat particularly, I have a record. People can see what I have fought for. They can watch past commission meetings and know that you'll not find a better fighter for, you know, our district," Baxter said.Baxter also noted that decisions before the County Commission involve seven commissioners, each bringing their own opinions to the table.On one of the most controversial development issues in western Palm Beach County, Baxter and Waldron find themselves on the same side.Both candidates have opposed Project Tango, the proposal for a massive AI data center near the Arden community and a new elementary school.The issue has become part of a broader conversation over data center development in Palm Beach County and what that development could mean for surrounding communities.For Waldron, the Project Tango debate also connects to her broader argument about transparency and how development decisions affect residents.For Baxter, the issue is part of the record she is asking voters to consider as she seeks another term representing District 6.After discussing their differences, Hoffman closed each interview with a different question: What is one thing each candidate respects about her opponent?"I respect anybody who wants to serve the public and represent the public," Waldron told Hoffman.Waldron said she believes elected officials can sometimes face criticism without people appreciating the challenges that come with serving in public office."A lot of times people bash politicians or leaders and stuff like that. And a lot of times, I don't think it's really fair," Waldron said."You can have tough days, and I imagine she's probably had some," Waldron added.Baxter expressed a similar view about the difficulty of representing residents with different opinions."It's definitely not as easy as people might think," Baxter told Hoffman. "You have people with different opinions, as we should. So you're always going to have somebody who's upset because they don't like that, and your people are going to be happy because they like what you stand for.""At the end of the day, we do our best to represent the residents," Baxter said.Despite their differences over how District 6 should be represented, Baxter and Waldron agree on one thing as the race nears its end: They want residents to get out and vote.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. King tides are pushing water onto roads across the Treasure Coast , and forecasters say the high water isn’t done yet. The National Weather Service extended a coastal flood warning for Martin, St. Lucie and Indian River counties until 2 a.m. The warning first took effect early Sunday and was originally set to expire Monday night. In Sewall’s Point, Sewall’s Point Road was completely flooded Wednesday. Cars and trucks crawled through the water, and several vehicles got stuck. Gina Rossi-Scheiman lives just around the corner. She has dealt with king tides before, but she says nothing like this. The flooding is really bad right now. I didn’t expect it to be this bad where I’m really not comfortable going down the road, Rossi-Scheiman said. She said Sewall’s Point Road is narrow to begin with, which makes the flooding harder to get around. The road isn’t this bad often, but when it is, you really can’t be out in it, she said. If your car is lower to the ground, you can’t drive in it at all. She worries her car could stall in the water and that the saltwater will damage it, so she plans to stay home unless she has to go out. The flooding stretched well beyond Sewall’s Point . Parts of South Hutchinson Island were underwater, and Northeast Indian River Drive flooded during high tide. In Palm City, the Martin County Sheriff’s Office reported significant flooding along Southwest Dyer Point Road, Southwest 34th Street and Cornell Avenue. In Fort Pierce, the high water carried a dumpster out into the water. King tides are exceptionally high tides that happen around a full or new moon, when the pull of the sun and moon line up and lift the water higher than usual. This round came around Sunday night’s full moon. Strong onshore winds piled even more water against the coast, sending it over seawalls and into low-lying neighborhoods. See also: Corvette, Ferrari take baths as king tides flood West Palm Beach, Lantana Some relief is on the way, but not right away. CBS12 meteorologists expect the winds to ease through the rest of the week. Even with calmer conditions, the tides will stay high enough to keep pushing water into flood-prone streets around high tide. The weather service warns that coastal roads may close and that low-lying homes, businesses and some critical infrastructure could flood. Forecasters also expect significant shoreline erosion. Coastal flooding is occurring or imminent, the weather service said in its latest statement. The beaches remain dangerous as well. A high surf advisory is in effect until 2 a.m. Friday, with breaking waves of 7 to 11 feet. A high rip current risk runs through late Friday night, and forecasters urge swimmers to stay out of the water. Rossi-Scheiman is finding some humor in it. She joked that her husband, who drives a low car, might have to sleep at work. But that’d be okay with me, she said. Officials urge drivers to stay off flooded roads, since there’s no telling how deep the water is.

What looks like an ordinary blue backpack is giving first responders in North Palm Beach a new way to connect with people with autism during an emergency.North Palm Beach Fire Rescue has equipped its fire trucks with Ben's Blue Bags, backpacks filled with sensory and communication tools designed to help first responders interact with people experiencing sensory overstimulation.WATCH REPORT BELOW: North Palm Beach firefighters add sensory bags for autism callsThe bags can include items such as fidget toys, noise-canceling headphones, dry-erase boards, and communication tools that can help someone express what they need or how they are feeling."Fidget toys, fidget spinners, Rubik's Cubes," firefighter Noah Denker said while showing WPTV reporter Christy Waite what is inside one of the bags. "The special thing about these bags is they have communication devices. There's a blank white board they can write on, there's a keyboard so they can type it out, and a how are you feeling chart."For Denker, bringing the bags to North Palm Beach started with a connection close to home. His wife is a fifth-grade teacher who works with children with autism. Seeing how she uses sensory tools with her students inspired Denker to find a way to give first responders similar resources in the field."My wife is a fifth-grade teacher for kids with autism, and she gave me the idea," Denker said. "She has things in her classroom to help with overstimulation before they hit that meltdown stage."That idea led Denker to research Ben's Blue Bags.Ben's Blue Bags is a nonprofit that was founded in 2019 by Matt Kodicek, a captain and paramedic with the Crown Point Fire Department in Indiana and the father of a child on the autism spectrum. The idea was inspired by his son, Ben, after Kodicek saw a need for first responders to have additional tools and training to help people experiencing sensory overstimulation.The organization has distributed more than 700 bags, and they are being used by more than 3,000 first responders across seven states and Canada.Now, some of those bags are riding along on North Palm Beach fire trucks, giving crews immediate access to sensory and communication tools when they respond to a call. The department says North Palm Beach Fire Rescue is the first department in Florida to use Ben's Blue Bags. "We are seeing more and more kids with autism or at least on the spectrum, so we think they will have a big impact when it comes time for us to use them," North Palm Beach Fire Rescue Deputy Chief Anthony Giarrusso said.The department is also hoping the effort eventually extends beyond fire rescue.Denker said they are working with the North Palm Beach Police Department to get the bags into the hands of police officers, giving both agencies access to the tools when they encounter someone who may need them.

For years, Palm Beach County has faced a shortage of mental health resources for children, leaving families vulnerable. Now, members of the community are stepping up to fill the need.Florida Atlantic University is launching a new program to provide that support for free.WATCH REPORT BELOW: FAU launches free mental health program for childrenThe program, called "OWLS-FLY" (short for Opportunity, Wellness, Leadership & Strength with Families Leading Youth), is being spearheaded by researchers Kelly Emelianchik-Key and Alex Fields inside the education building at FAU. It was made possible by a $1.2 million grant from the Children's Services Council of Palm Beach County.The program will provide free mental health counseling for kids ages 6 through 17 and their families."We provide group counseling, individual counseling, family counseling, and we'll have some different parental supports that are going to take place," Emelianchik-Key said.The space is still coming together with different rooms for family and individual therapy. There's also a room set up to provide care via telehealth. Emelianchik-Key said she anticipates the first clients to be served in January.Fields said the stakes for young people are high."If you don't have solid mental health support, you can't build the foundation for a really healthy and high quality of life down the road," Fields said.The program serves two needs: it helps families who need services, and it provides work experience for the people who are learning to provide them."We've worked with clinicians in the community, specifically for youth with intellectual and developmental disabilities, and I've heard how long their wait lists are, and that they're not able to provide services for months and on out," Fields said.Master's students and graduates will get work experience through the program. Michelle Abarca of the Children's Services Council hopes to take what's learned through FAU's program and scale it in the future."Working with FAU is particularly exciting for us because we are a data-driven organization, and with the research that's going to be taking place at FAU, we hope to learn. We hope to be able to replicate some of this at one point," Abarca said.The program is funded for three years, but Emelianchik-Key and Fields hope to continue it for years to come."To be able to do this is a really great honor," Emelianchik-Key said.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. In Florida, you can find a good football game anywhere, but few schools have both great football and amazing band play like Palm Beach Lakes Community High School."Seven-time MVP, seven-time FNBC Champs, and seven-time superior-rated band," said Jazz Velez, the band president.WATCH REPORT BELOW: Palm Beach Lakes band shines on and off field If you don’t know what that means, let me put it: the Ram Regiment is the best band in the state."It’s an amazing feeling, but it's a lot of pressure sometimes because we have to put on a show every time we go out there," said Velez.They put on a show, alright.They've won the state championship, they're the No. 1 superior-rated band in West Palm Beach, and are fresh from a trip to London for the 2026 New Year's Day Parade.If you still don't believe how good they are, the school's quarterback, Jordan Johnson, has one wish ahead of every home and away game: will the band be there?"The band means everything to our culture. The Indian River State College Board of Trustees has delayed taking action on a recommendation to eliminate the college's swimming and diving team.During a meeting held in Okeechobee, the board voted Tuesday to table the president's recommendation to eliminate the program.WATCH REPORT BELOW: IRSC trustees table recommendation to eliminate swimming, diving teamInstead, trustees asked the college administration to prepare a comprehensive report on the swimming and diving program. The board requested that the report include input from the community.President Timothy Moore said at Tuesday's meeting that the proposal to cut the programs comes down to money."It's a tremendous opportunity to leave this college with that kind of skill, resource and talent here, but it comes at a price," Moore said.The school president said the program currently costs around $1.4 to $2 million, money that isn't coming in through donations."What's required to maintain it as it sits today? We will require $15 to $20 million of an endowment to throw off enough revenue per year to sustain the program as it sits today," Moore said.There's also a proposal to transition the remaining sports to Division II, resulting in potential savings of around $500,000.But if the swimming and diving program stays, Moore said the school may be forced to cut 50 percent for sports across the board."It's elimination of one or impose a penalty across all, and I would imagine that our championships will suffer because of that decision," Moore said.The administration is expected to present the report at the Board of Trustees Nov. 17 meeting, when recommendations on how to move forward will be considered.This past March, the men's swim and dive team captured its 52nd consecutive national championship title, and the women's team claimed its 48th crown.Former swimmer Ella Smith started a petition last week to save the program, which has more than 12,500 signatures.

Women's hockey is growing in South Florida, from the pee-wee level all the way up to the college level, and the University of Miami Women's Hockey Club team is part of that surge.Head coach Justina Holland, a former player, rebooted the women's hockey club program at the University of Miami in 2021. She rebuilt it from the ground up, taking on every task herself as a college student.WATCH BELOW: Women's hockey growing at University of Miami"Yes, all by myself. I had to find some girls that wanted to play. I did buy jerseys, get ice time, like everything. Every single little thing you can think of, I had to do myself," Holland said.At first, the team had only six players and no subs, and they competed in a women's league. "We didn't even have any colleges to play against. You're playing against grown women, and that was a little bit humbling, but we had a lot of fun, and that was kind of the start of your year. So from there, it kind of picked up. The year after, we had UT Tampa, USF; they joined. Then we got it going, and you get teams like Georgia, Alabama, Auburn, and we're slowly building up the South to what it is right now," Holland said.This year, the Canes have 14 players, and Holland credits social media for helping to spread the word and getting more students on skates. "It's everything we gained almost 7,000 followers within like a month," Holland said.With more people seeing the pictures and videos they post on Instagram, the more support they see. Co-captain Alex Meola wants the team to become a flagship club on campus and says the camaraderie is what makes it special."We just have such a good time with each other. It's like it's hard not to. And that's the beautiful thing about club sports is like it brings you back to that first initial reason why you started playing hockey, right?" Meola said.With more and more interest in skating the club's way, Holland says anyone can gear up."You don't have to be the best player ever. We have girls from all different levels. So it's more of like if you know how to play, you want to play, like come join. That's kind of the vibe: to have fun," Holland said.

After noticing worsening water quality while rowing, South Fork High School senior Bianca Bernhard founded the Martin Oyster Restoration Initiative (MORI) a student-led nonprofit that recycles oyster shells to support restoration projects in local waterways.“The water quality got really bad,” Bernhard told WPTV’s T.A. “That’s due to discharges from Lake Okeechobee, so I decided to do something with the extra free time.”The initiative, known as MORI, collects oyster shells from local restaurants. Volunteers at South Fork High School then help dry and cure the shells so they can be used in restoration projects.WATCH: Stuart student leads oyster restoration mission“I recycle a lot of shells from local restaurants,” Bernhard said. “These local shells will help create new reef structures like what I’m holding right here, and those reef structures will grow new oysters which will filter the water.”South Fork High School students and teachers have joined Bernhard’s conservation effort through the school’s marine science, construction and agriculture programs.During the WPTV segment, Jennifer Inostroza, a teacher at South Fork High School, explained that the school helps cure and dry the oyster shells so they are ready for future projects.Information provided by the Martin County School District says MORI has recruited more than 60 students and teachers and amassed approximately 1,600 pounds of oyster shell.The district says participating students can earn honor credits through South Fork High School’s Marine Sciences program.The recycled shells do not immediately return to the water. They must first be transported, dried and cured before they can be incorporated into approved restoration structures.According to Bernhard, those structures provide places where new oysters can grow. She said the oysters then help filter and clean the surrounding water.MORI is also collaborating with Docks for a Clean Lagoon, a nonprofit that installs vertical oyster gardens. According to Bernhard’s Go Blue Awards narrative, shells cured by South Fork volunteers have been used in the creation of vertical oyster gardens intended for the Indian River Lagoon.Bernhard is a finalist in the Blue Hatchling Youth category of Loggerhead Marinelife Center’s 2026 Go Blue Awards.“Bianca is one of our finalists for the Go Blue Hatchling Awards,” said Audrey Padgett, VP of Marketing, at Loggerhead Marinelife Center, told WPTV. “We’ve had nominees from all over the world. So it’s really amazing to see someone selected by this independent panel of judges here in our backyard for the work that she’s doing to improve ocean conservation and ecosystems right here.”The annual awards recognize young people, individuals, businesses and nonprofit organizations making contributions to ocean conservation.The 2026 Go Blue Awards ceremony is scheduled for 11:30 a.m. 30, at the Kravis Center for the Performing Arts in West Palm Beach.Bernhard’s work comes as MORI prepares for its next phase. According to her Go Blue Awards narrative, she aims to expand the initiative to three additional local schools during the 2026-27 school year.She also plans to pursue oyster restoration research with the Florida Oceanographic Society and work with students to develop additional structures for restoration projects.For Bernhard, the project began with something she saw while rowing. It has since grown into a broader effort that gives students a hands-on role in responding to the environmental challenges facing their community.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Three seniors at Alexander W. Dreyfoos School of the Arts have created Prodigy Pro, a free artificial intelligence platform designed to help students turn their ideas into real-world ventures.Co-founders Aiden Azoy and Anthony Tan and Head of Design Mia Rubio developed the platform after attending South Florida business networking events and realizing how few students were in the room.WATCH: Dreyfoos seniors build free AI platform for student entrepreneurs“We attended networking events and we noticed, why are we the youngest people in the room?” Azoy said. “There are so many talented students in our communities where they’re able to pursue their professional careers outside of school.”The students said they wanted to give young people a way to explore their interests, develop practical ideas and participate in West Palm Beach’s growing business community.The founders attend Dreyfoos in downtown West Palm Beach, where new development and the arrival of major companies have fueled the area’s growing reputation as “Wall Street South.”“We go to Dreyfoos, and literally hundreds of feet away are these huge constructions of Related Ross, companies like ServiceNow or even Citadel moving down to South Florida,” Tan said. “We’re right at the forefront of this new business center that is becoming West Palm Beach.”Tan said the students attempted to connect with professionals at local gatherings but struggled to find opportunities intended for people their age.“We tried to go to these meetings, and a lot of the time there wouldn’t be any opportunity for us,” Tan said. “So that’s why we wanted to create our own.”Prodigy Pro was built to help students take the first steps toward developing projects and businesses.“Prodigy Pro is a free AI entrepreneurship platform that helps a student take their idea from an idea to the final product,” Tan said.Azoy said the team created the platform after noticing that many students were not taking their ideas beyond the classroom.“Prodigy Pro is a way for students to build real ventures outside of school and be able to pursue their professional interests,” Azoy said. “We noticed that not enough students are getting out there and really putting their ideas out into the world. We gave them the ability to do that.”Users enter information about an idea and the problem they hope to solve. The platform’s AI then helps organize the concept and identify potential next steps.Rubio designed the user interface and worked to make the process understandable for students who may have little or no previous business experience.“You upload your information and the idea that you really want to pursue,” Rubio said. “And the AI will help you guide and shape and really tell you what your next step is, as well as create roadmaps, reminders and just really help your venture get off the ground.”The platform divides the development process into smaller sections and tasks.“With Prodigy [Pro], we wanted to make the next step super easy and attainable,” Rubio said. “So we grouped things into different sections and made each task super easy for the user to understand, so they know what to do next with their venture.”During a demonstration, the students used concerns about a school bus route to show how a user could enter a problem and explore possible efficiencies. “You input your information, and it really gives you the next steps, what you should do, and you can ask the AI to help develop your venture,” Rubio said.The founders said making Prodigy Pro free was central to their mission. Azoy said students should have access to the same entrepreneurial tools regardless of their school or community’s resources.“It’s completely free for students, and we want to stress that because we want to basically give the message that a student in an underprivileged school or community should have the same exact resources as, you know, a student in a resourced school,” Azoy said.According to the students, Prodigy Pro has grown to more than 15,000 users in 20 countries.The team also competed in the Mott Million Dollar Challenge, a national student entrepreneurship competition.“A few months ago in May, we competed in the Mott Million Dollar Challenge, where we won $7,500 for our venture,” Tan said.Tan said the prize money was reinvested into Prodigy Pro.“A lot of it went into the development of the platform, going through the UI, the back end, also enabling the AI to be free for other students,” he said.The three founders are seniors preparing for life after high school, but they said Prodigy Pro will continue.Asked whether the platform would remain after graduation, Rubio responded, “Yes, of course. It’ll remain to be a free platform for our users.”For Azoy, the larger goal is to show young people that they do not have to wait to begin developing their professional interests.“We really think that it’s important for them to be showing up and, you know, building ventures that really matter because every student has creativity in an underprivileged or privileged school,” Azoy said.The students’ work comes as artificial intelligence becomes increasingly integrated into education, business and everyday problem-solving. By making the platform free, the Dreyfoos seniors hope more young people will be able to turn their creativity into action and create opportunities of their own.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Blue Repose Foundation is launching a pilot program designed to help law enforcement officers and other public safety professionals recover from occupational stress through weekly float sessions, peer support and coping techniques.The startup nonprofit introduced the program at Float8 in Delray Beach, where Blue Repose Founder and President Bridget Coghlan discussed the pressures public safety professionals can encounter and the stigma that may prevent some from seeking support.“With our field, of course, we're exposed to traumas, long shift hours, and things of that nature,” Coghlan said. “We don't like to say mental health, so we just want to take care of the person and give them resources to do so within their professional life and their personal life at home.”Coghlan said the pilot will include five participants during its initial monthlong run at Transitions Wellness and Performance Center in Juno Beach.“They'll get a float session, one per week, followed by peer support and other coping decompression techniques to follow and hopefully it'll help them out,” Coghlan said.The program is part of Blue Repose Foundation’s developing mission to provide private, nonclinical restorative opportunities to law enforcement officers, corrections professionals and others working in public safety.Blue Repose says the foundation is being established in Martin County, with an initial focus on serving the Treasure Coast and Palm Beach County. Kristen Neves, the foundation’s director of community engagement and partnerships, said Blue Repose is seeking financial support to launch the pilot.“We're really looking for the community support right now to fund this program and get this pilot program up and going,” Neves said. “We just really want to get this out there and get those law enforcement supported.”Information about contributing to the program is available on the Blue Repose Foundation website.Float8 owner Matt Beck said the Delray Beach studio uses float cabins rather than pods.Float cabins contain shallow water with a high concentration of Epsom salt, allowing a person to remain buoyant. The private environment also reduces outside light, sound and other stimulation.“By reducing the effects of gravity and external stimulation on the body, it helps induce a meditative state, downregulate your nervous system, and help you recover from those stressful situations that our law enforcement officers face so often,” Beck said.Blue Repose describes the float experience as one component of a broader program that will include peer support and additional coping and decompression techniques.Public safety professionals can encounter trauma, long shifts, and sustained stress while serving their communities. Blue Repose’s pilot reflects an effort to give participants structured time to decompress while connecting them with support beyond the float cabin.The initial program will allow Blue Repose to begin evaluating its approach with a small group of participants as the nonprofit works to secure community funding.The foundation’s broader goal is to help professionals take care of themselves in both their working and personal lives while making recovery a more accepted part of public service.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI.
