A data breach involving a Florida student financial aid website may have exposed personal information, including Social Security numbers, belonging to approximately 4.9 million people, according to the Florida Department of Education (FLDOE).FLDOE said in a Thursday statement that staff became aware Oct. 19 of unauthorized criminal access involving its Florida Student Financial Aid website.The department said the compromised personally identifiable information included Social Security numbers. Officials did not specify what other types of personal information may have been exposed.The breach is believed to have been limited to the Florida Student Financial Aid website, and as many as 4.9 million people potentially were affected, according to FLDOE.The department said it activated its cybersecurity response protocols after detecting the incident, took steps to contain the unauthorized activity and secure its systems, and notified the Florida Attorney General's Office.FLDOE said it is working with the Florida Digital Service and Florida Department of Law Enforcement. The incident remains under criminal investigation.FLDOE said current financial aid is not at risk and the incident will not delay financial aid disbursements or tuition payments from the department.Officials also said the breach will not affect eligibility for scholarships, grants or student loans from FLDOE.Some department websites and online services, however, may experience temporary disruptions as officials work to restore full functionality.FLDOE recommends monitoring financial and online accounts for suspicious activity and regularly reviewing account statements and credit reports.The department also recommends considering a fraud alert or credit freeze with the major credit bureaus. Consumers can obtain free credit reports through AnnualCreditReport.com and find additional information about responding to a data breach through the Federal Trade Commission's IdentityTheft.gov website.Anyone with questions about the FLDOE breach can contact the department at databreach@fldoe.org.FLDOE said information could change as the criminal investigation continues. The department is posting updates on its data breach information page.

Martin County commissioners unanimously voted during a second public hearing to implement a one-year moratorium on large-scale data center applications, giving staff time to study potential environmental impacts and establish rules for future projects. During the hearing, every resident who spoke during public comment opposed the possibility of data centers in the county. "We simply do not have enough information on what we may be introducing to this ecologically sensitive region and the world's most extensive restoration effort. We need more study and the evaluation of potential impacts, especially in the 16-county greater Everglades region," said Casey Darling, policy director for Friends of the Everglades. "I don’t want to spend another year or longer where somebody that I know is trying to do me great bodily harm. Folks, it’s in your hands. These things are not to be near people that are trying to conduct their ordinary lives," said resident Richard Miller. Commissioner Blake Capps confirmed there is an applicant for a data center. "One of them is the Florida Gateway Project, where this one project has been ... a data center application has come on Kanner Highway," Capps said. A resident who lives near the proposed site raised concerns about the scale of the project. "I happen to live one mile from this new proposed mega center, 100 MW, and 100 MW is like unbelievable to power 100,000 homes, and that's going to be a mile from me. Who knows how much water it's going to use," the resident said. Commissioner Vargas expressed frustration with the application process. "I was not too happy about hearing this application. I even requested the receipt, which I have here in my hand, and the date ... We should give them back and say they don't want you here. It's okay, you go elsewhere," Vargas said. The application for the Florida Gateway Project was submitted on Oct. 12, with the first public hearing held the following day. "We got the information late on the Monday before the 13th ... so, I didn't have the information in advance of the 13th. At the meeting on the 13th, I disclosed to everybody that I had just found out about it. I'm sorry, Commissioner, we did alert the commission as soon as we could," said County Attorney Elysse A. "I understand, but somebody took the money on this date is what I'm trying to say. Doesn't anybody talk to anybody here?" Vargas said. The application will go through the development review process, which staff said is expected to take a year. Aside from this application, there are currently no other large-scale data center applications pending. King tides are pushing water onto roads across the Treasure Coast , and forecasters say the high water isn’t done yet. The National Weather Service extended a coastal flood warning for Martin, St. Lucie and Indian River counties until 2 a.m. The warning first took effect early Sunday and was originally set to expire Monday night. In Sewall’s Point, Sewall’s Point Road was completely flooded Wednesday. Cars and trucks crawled through the water, and several vehicles got stuck. Gina Rossi-Scheiman lives just around the corner. She has dealt with king tides before, but she says nothing like this. The flooding is really bad right now. I didn’t expect it to be this bad where I’m really not comfortable going down the road, Rossi-Scheiman said. She said Sewall’s Point Road is narrow to begin with, which makes the flooding harder to get around. The road isn’t this bad often, but when it is, you really can’t be out in it, she said. If your car is lower to the ground, you can’t drive in it at all. She worries her car could stall in the water and that the saltwater will damage it, so she plans to stay home unless she has to go out. The flooding stretched well beyond Sewall’s Point . Parts of South Hutchinson Island were underwater, and Northeast Indian River Drive flooded during high tide. In Palm City, the Martin County Sheriff’s Office reported significant flooding along Southwest Dyer Point Road, Southwest 34th Street and Cornell Avenue. In Fort Pierce, the high water carried a dumpster out into the water. King tides are exceptionally high tides that happen around a full or new moon, when the pull of the sun and moon line up and lift the water higher than usual. This round came around Sunday night’s full moon. Strong onshore winds piled even more water against the coast, sending it over seawalls and into low-lying neighborhoods. See also: Corvette, Ferrari take baths as king tides flood West Palm Beach, Lantana Some relief is on the way, but not right away. CBS12 meteorologists expect the winds to ease through the rest of the week. Even with calmer conditions, the tides will stay high enough to keep pushing water into flood-prone streets around high tide. The weather service warns that coastal roads may close and that low-lying homes, businesses and some critical infrastructure could flood. Forecasters also expect significant shoreline erosion. Coastal flooding is occurring or imminent, the weather service said in its latest statement. The beaches remain dangerous as well. A high surf advisory is in effect until 2 a.m. Friday, with breaking waves of 7 to 11 feet. A high rip current risk runs through late Friday night, and forecasters urge swimmers to stay out of the water. Rossi-Scheiman is finding some humor in it. She joked that her husband, who drives a low car, might have to sleep at work. But that’d be okay with me, she said. Officials urge drivers to stay off flooded roads, since there’s no telling how deep the water is.

Nearly eight years after WPTV first investigated concerns about a possible cluster of glioblastoma cases in St. Lucie County, health officials have reviewed the numbers again.The latest findings show the number of cases remains in line with what would be expected based on the county's population, but families who lost loved ones to the deadly brain cancer say important questions remain unanswered.WATCH THE REPORT BELOW: The latest review by the Florida Department of Health follows years of WPTV reporting into concerns raised by patients and families who discovered they lived near others diagnosed with the same aggressive form of brain cancer.While health officials say the data does not show a statistically significant increase in cases, the review does not examine whether patients were concentrated on particular streets or in specific neighborhoods.For families who have spent years searching for answers, that distinction matters.READ THE FULL STATE REPORT BELOW: A young man's death helped spark an investigationFor Deb Johnston, the loss of her son, Lenny Schelin Jr., is still painful."It's been eight years since Lenny passed," she said.Lenny was just 33 years old when he died from glioblastoma, one of the most aggressive forms of brain cancer.He was healthy, active and loved fishing. He survived just 17 months after his diagnosis."Everybody loved Lenny. He just had this charm about him," his mother recalled.Lenny's story was among the first that helped WPTV uncover concerns about glioblastoma cases in St. Lucie County.Other patients included Mark Cunningham, who was also in his 30s, and Kyle Vericella, who was just 18.After WPTV anchor Meghan McRoberts uncovered the local cases, dozens of additional patients and family members contacted her with their stories.Area doctors and neurosurgeons also expressed concerns.Glioblastoma is most commonly diagnosed in older adults, making the younger ages of some patients particularly troubling to their families.But it wasn't just their ages that raised questions.As patients began connecting with one another, WPTV mapped where they lived beginning in 2018.Some lived within blocks of one another. Others lived on the same street. In one case, unrelated patients had lived in the same home.The reporting drew attention from lawmakers, environmental advocate Erin Brockovich and the Florida Department of Health.What did the original 2019 investigation find?The concerns prompted health officials to examine glioblastoma cases in St. Lucie County."You brought it to my attention. It was alarming; it was nerve-wracking," Clint Sperber, administrator for the Florida Department of Health in St. Lucie County, told WPTV's Meghan McRoberts.Sperber said the concerns led to a request for assistance from Florida's cancer registry."I asked for assistance from our cancer registry through our leadership, my boss," he said. "And we were able to help collect a lot of information."That information was compiled into a report released in 2019.Despite concerns about the number of patients diagnosed with glioblastoma, the report did not find a statistically significant increase in cases that would warrant a more intensive investigation.Health officials also reviewed existing environmental monitoring information, including public water utility data and radiation monitoring records associated with the area's power plant.Sperber pointed to ongoing environmental monitoring as part of the state's assessment."There is water testing, there is vegetation testing, they look at watermelon, milk, fish, soil, they would know if there is any release of radiation," Sperber said.The findings were disappointing for families who had hoped the investigation would uncover an explanation."I was like deflated because we worked so hard," Johnston said.What does the latest glioblastoma review show?Seven years after the original report, health officials have taken another look at glioblastoma cases in St. Lucie County.Their conclusion remains largely unchanged."The conclusion that was found in 2019 is the same one we have today," Sperber told WPTV. "We are seeing the same ratio, the same expected number of cases that we would expect statewide for our county."According to Sperber, a county with approximately 400,000 residents would be expected to see about 14 to 15 new glioblastoma diagnoses each year.The report also shows that from 2019 to 2023, there were 95 cases of glioblastoma, just three cases more than the 92 expected.Health officials say the latest review does not identify an unusual increase in glioblastoma cases compared with statewide expectations.Unlike the 2019 report, however, the latest review does not break down cases by age or sex.Officials say there are too few cases to make those comparisons statistically reliable.The review also considered existing water and radiation monitoring records without identifying new concerns.What questions remain?Although the latest review did not find an unusual increase in glioblastoma cases countywide, it does not settle every question raised by patients and their families.Sperber acknowledged the analysis does not closely examine whether patients lived near one another on particular streets or within specific neighborhoods.That means the review's broader findings do not necessarily address the geographic patterns that originally concerned families, determining what causes glioblastoma is also challenging.Sperber pointed to recent research by the International Journal of Molecular Sciences identifying nearly a dozen potential factors associated with the disease, making it difficult to identify a single environmental source."I wish there was an answer," Sperber said. "I wish there was a smoking gun that says okay here is the reason, the cause, the source for glioblastoma."As St. Lucie County's population continues to grow, health officials expect the total number of diagnoses to rise as well.But for families who lost loved ones, the question remains whether the countywide numbers tell the entire story.A mother's call for a closer look at her hometownFor Johnston, hearing that the state's findings have not changed was difficult."I was deflated when you told me that. I was like, oh my God," she told McRoberts.She remains grateful that health officials are continuing to review the numbers.When asked whether she was glad the state was still looking into the issue, she responded, "Yes … it gives you hope for the others that come behind us."But she wants investigators to look more closely at individual neighborhoods, rather than relying on broader geographic data.When McRoberts asked where she would like additional testing conducted, her answer was immediate."In the White City area," she said.Nearly eight years after losing her son, Deb says the search for answers has taken an emotional toll."I haven't given up; it's just you get tired," she said.Millions invested in glioblastoma researchSince WPTV's initial reporting, the Florida Department of Health has invested at least $9 million in glioblastoma research.Deb has also worked to support research in her son's memory.Each year, she hosts a fishing tournament honoring Lenny, who loved spending time on the water.The event has raised nearly $300,000 for glioblastoma research.Another tournament is approaching, continuing her efforts to help other families facing the same devastating diagnosis.For Deb, the hope is that continued research and closer examination of local cases will eventually provide answers."I'm just glad you have followed through the way that you have," she told McRoberts.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Lucie man was arrested on charges alleging he threatened to file lawsuits and ethics complaints against State Rep. Meg Weinberger unless she publicly apologized and backed his push for government audits, according to a Palm Beach County Sheriff's Offic e probable cause affidavit. Anthony Pizzarelli, 50, was booked Oct. He faces charges of extortion, using a two-way communication device to facilitate a felony, and harassing an elected official, according to the affidavit. The charges are allegations; Pizzarelli is presumed innocent unless proven guilty. Investigators say Pizzarelli emailed Weinberger on Feb. 9 and offered to leave her out of lawsuits and ethics complaints he said he planned to file if she issued a swift public apology. He also proposed wording for the apology. In an April 6 email, he allegedly renewed the threat, writing that he did not plan to name her in the complaints but that can change, and urged her to help with his audit campaign. According to the affidavit, Pizzarelli transmitted a voice memo May 18th, 2026, directly to Weinberger's personal cell phone in which he stated, among other things: "I'm an angry person, so I'm not being nice," "I'm doing the lawsuits," and "you don't know what I can do." The affidavit says Pizzarelli wanted Weinberger to support audits of Palm Beach and St. Lucie counties and pursue investigations into government contracting. Weinberger told investigators she had never met him, did not represent him and had no authority over St. She said she viewed the messages as threats and feared for her safety and her family’s, according to the affidavit. Pizzarelli told investigators he viewed his communications as good faith notices and denied using them to leverage Weinberger. He said he was seeking an apology over an incident in which she had been copied on an email, and was trying to get her support for his complaints. He had not filed a lawsuit or ethics complaint against her at the time of his interview, the affidavit says. See also: Florida woman convicted in $8.6 million Medicare fraud scheme The affidavit says the investigation found probable cause for the charges after reviewing emails, a May voice message and evidence from electronic devices. Prior accusation of threats In 2025, Pizzarelli was accused of sending threatening emails to St. Lucie County commissioners. Deputies say the communications escalated in tone and content, which raised concern among officials. In the emails he sent, he allegedly using threatening language that included being "ruthless" and making allusions to "murder charges where applicable." Pizzarelli was arrested and booked on counts of intimidation - sending written threats to kill or injure. In the current affidavit, Pizzarelli told investigators that all charges from the 2025 case had been dropped. Weinberger, running for reelection, faced intimidation in 2024 Weinberger, a first-term Republican, represents Florida House District 94 in Palm Beach County, according to the Florida House. Weinberger’s campaign faced a separate voter intimidation case during the 2024 election. Nicholas Farley was arrested after a campaign volunteer said he yelled antisemitic slurs at her and drove threateningly near early voters outside the Acreage Branch Library. Farley told detectives that seeing Weinberger campaign posters triggered his remarks. The case involved Farley, not Pizzarelli. Absolutely it’s very scary we’re dealing with this. It’s just no way to live and maybe he opens his eyes and realize that we’re just all people doesn’t matter your religion or skin color, Weinberger said at the time. Weinberger is seeking reelection on Tuesday. She faces Democrat Elizabeth Holmes and Doug Barrow (no party affiliation). House District 94 is entirely within Palm Beach County. It stretches from the western Glades communities of Belle Glade, Pahokee and South Bay through areas such as Westlake, Loxahatchee Groves, The Acreage and Jupiter Farms, and includes parts of several eastern communities, including West Palm Beach, Palm Beach Gardens, Jupiter and Royal Palm Beach.

Family and friends are mourning St. Lucie County firefighter Austin Hodge, a man those closest to him describe as endlessly positive and devoted to serving his community. A funeral procession for Hodge left the Medical Examiner’s Office in Fort Pierce at 2 p.m. Monday and traveled to Stone Brothers Funeral Home. Lucie County Sheriff's Office went to the station at 7:25 a.m. 24, regarding a "full cardiac arrest," and Hoge was taken to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital. His death comes about 15 months after his younger brother, Jarius Hodge, also a St. Lucie County Fire District firefighter and paramedic, died in July 2025 after falling ill during a shift. The district honored Jarius with line-of-duty honors. After his brother’s death, Austin spent months searching for answers. He told CBS12 News in January that Jarius caught the flu from a patient and died hours after arriving at Cleveland Clinic Tradition Hospital in Port St. Lucie, struggling to breathe. Austin said medical records showed doctors made critical mistakes, including needing three attempts to intubate his brother. CBS12 reached out to the hospital at the time and did not receive a response before that story was published. Because Jarius was over 25 and had no spouse or children, Florida’s so-called free kill law barred his family from suing for medical malpractice. Austin pushed state lawmakers to repeal it and started a petition in his brother’s honor. He said the fight was about accountability, not money. Bernard Taylor has known Austin since their school days in Sebastian. Taylor was a senior and Austin a freshman when they met at the Boys and Girls Club, where Taylor worked as a counselor and Austin was one of the kids he mentored. Taylor said Austin always wanted to keep up with the older kids, and the two formed a bond that lasted for years. Later, when Taylor decided to change careers, Austin was one of the first people he called. Taylor said Austin supported him through becoming a firefighter, from answering questions to helping him with his conditioning. Just a ball of positive energy. A smile that lights up the room. No matter what you’re going through, he had the right words to kind of get you through it, Taylor said. Taylor said he spoke with Austin about a week before his death to make sure he was doing well. He said he is most heartbroken for Austin’s mother, who has now lost both of her sons. That’s one of the strongest people I’ve ever met in my life. I don’t know if I can hold it together if I was her, Taylor said. Bonnie Hill, a family friend who helped raise Austin’s mother, said she has been by her side and that the family is leaning on its faith and a strong circle of support. I say on my watch, I’m not going to let you die. You’re going to live, and we’re going to get through this, Hill said of what she has told Austin’s mother. Hill said that faith is what is carrying the family now. See also: King tides cause coastal flooding, beach closures in Palm Beach County and Treasure Coast We believe God even in this. We believe God, and we stand on the promises because they won’t fail, Hill said. Taylor said he hopes people remember Austin for his love of serving others. He was a person who loved what he did. He was a person who loved serving his community, Taylor said. Lucie County Fire District has not released details about Austin Hodge’s death.

Florida health officials notified CBS12 News on Thursday that an updated Treasure Coast brain cancer review is available, finding no statistically significant excess of glioblastoma in the areas examined. The findings come as the CBS12 News I-Team continues pressing the Florida Department of Health for updated data and answers about which brain tumors are counted. CBS12 News has covered families’ concerns for well over a decade. The analysis covers diagnoses through 2023, leaving more recent cases outside its scope. It also documents a change in the tumor classifications included compared with the state’s 2019 review. Lucie County Health Officer Clint Sperber directed the I-Team to the report, accompanying resources and a scientific journal article addressing environmental risk factors. I am hopeful that, after reviewing the website and the available documents, you will find reassurance in the thorough work conducted by our public health scientists, Sperber wrote. What the state found The updated assessment examined glioblastoma diagnoses from 2014 through 2023 in St. Lucie, Martin and Indian River counties, along with three St. Officials compared recorded diagnoses with the number expected based on statewide cancer rates, accounting for age. Lucie County, the state recorded 95 diagnoses from 2019 through 2023, compared with approximately 92 expected. Across the full decade, the ZIP code analysis found: 34952: 32 diagnoses, compared with approximately 26 expected. 34983: 21 diagnoses, compared with approximately 20 expected. 34982: 12 diagnoses, compared with approximately 13 expected. None showed a statistically significant excess. Officials said small case numbers can fluctuate by chance, while population growth can increase the number of diagnoses without an increase in underlying risk. The report does not determine what caused individual patients’ cancers. Questions beyond glioblastoma In June and October, I-Team reporter Katie Bente revisited families’ concerns, interviewing patients and traveling through neighborhoods with Stephanie Ankiel, who helps families through the Brain Cancer Foundation of the Treasure Coast. She pointed to her late husband’s childhood home in Fort Pierce and another home a few houses away where she said a resident received the same initial diagnosis in 2025: oligodendroglioma. Ankiel previously told CBS12 News that her husband, Mark Cunningham, was initially diagnosed with oligodendroglioma and that his cancer was later described as glioblastoma. The I-Team asked health officials how their analysis handles changing diagnoses and whether other brain cancers were examined separately. Those points were not explained in the department’s response before the report’s release. The updated report shows two tumor classification codes included in the 2019 analysis 9450 and 9451 were excluded from the new review. The department said evolving cancer classifications mean those codes are no longer included in the glioblastoma case definition. The report does not explain how cases initially classified as another tumor type and later described as glioblastoma are handled. Recent diagnoses fall outside the review The assessment does not include diagnoses from 2024 through 2026. An accompanying FAQ says 2023 was the latest finalized cancer registry year available. Officials said the reporting delay allows records to be checked for completeness and accuracy. That means the review does not capture diagnoses such as Laura Cooper’s. Lucie woman told CBS12 News in June that she was diagnosed with glioblastoma in November 2025, years after losing her best friend to the disease. At the time of the interview, she was undergoing treatment and participating in a clinical trial. Environmental records reviewed Health officials reviewed public drinking-water records, available private-well data and radiation monitoring around the St. Lucie nuclear power plant. The department reported that its water review did not identify contamination involving chemicals linked by the Environmental Protection Agency to glioblastoma or other brain-related health concerns. It also reported no increase in monitored environmental radiation levels around the plant. The documents describe reviews of existing records and monitoring data. They do not specify whether new environmental samples were collected specifically for this assessment. In Thursday’s email, Sperber highlighted the department’s conclusion that no environmental hazard in the Treasure Coast region has been shown to cause glioblastoma. The report also acknowledges limits to the cancer registry: It lacks environmental exposure information and complete residential histories. A patient’s address at diagnosis may not reflect where a relevant exposure occurred. The department said it will continue monitoring cancer incidence and working with state and local partners.

King tides and strong onshore winds have caused significant coastal erosion along the boardwalk in Vero Beach, with officials describing the damage as severe and warning that the weather event is not yet over. I was trying to look it up to see if there was a name, a named storm off the coast or anything, but nope, it's just weather," one observer said. Quintin Bergman is the resource manager with Indian River County. He's monitoring the situation. "So, what we're seeing here is two weather events that have aligned," Bergman said. "We're still in the middle of this. We're not through with the weather event. The forecast is showing elevated winds for a few more days, and the king tide event is still going to be affecting the tide." The erosion has impacted a section of beachfront parking on Ocean Drive, an area official have identified as one of their erosion hot spots. One couple who walked on the beach the day before said they didn’t notice the damage but weren’t surprised by the situation. "That's what nature wants to do, and that's kind of what you need to let nature do, I think. But the problem is we keep building on it. That's the interruption, not nature doing its thing," they said. Deep Dive: WPBF 25 News Investigates Officials described the erosion as approaching severe. "I would classify this as leaning more on the severe side of erosion. It's not extreme by any means, but definitely we are very concerned," Bergman said. Authorities are contacting park officials to discuss safety measures to protect the public. Lucie County, beach erosion has also been observed, but officials credited beach replenishment projects with helping protect nearby buildings. "I mean, it certainly helped that we did a renourishment last year. Any time you lose sand, the more you have on there, the better you're going to protect your shoreline," Erick Gill, St. Lucie County public information officer, said. In parts of Martin County, residents are still dealing with flooding caused by the rough conditions. Despite the challenges, some beachgoers in Vero Beach, like Svetlana Ryan, are still enjoying the view and noting the changes to the shoreline. "We noticed because there was so much sand before, and now it's just a wall. But you do with whatever you have to do here in Vero Beach," Ryan said. Officials plan to assess the damage after the weather event passes. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25

hero.headline: Viewing in Fort Pierce, memorial in Port St. Lucie announced for firefighter Austin Hodge
hero.body:
A public viewing in Fort Pierce and a memorial service in Port St. Lucie have been announced for St. Lucie County Fire District firefighter-paramedic Austin Hodge, who died in the line of duty Oct. 24. The district coordinated the arrangements with Hodge's family and Stone Brothers Funeral Home.

The public viewing will be held at River of Life Fellowship Church, located at 3950 Juanita Avenue in Fort Pierce. A memorial service will follow at Christ Fellowship Church, located at 10250 SW Village Parkway in Port St. Lucie.

Hodge served the St. Lucie County community for more than nine years, according to the fire district. “The St. Lucie County Fire District continues to mourn the loss of Firefighter/Paramedic Austin Hodge,” the agency said in a statement. “His loss is deeply felt by his family, friends, fellow firefighters, and the many lives he touched throughout his years of service.”

The district thanked the community for supporting Hodge's family and fellow firefighters following his death. “We remain grateful for the outpouring of love and support extended to Austin's family and our Fire District family during this difficult time,” the agency said.

hero.headline: Florida student aid breach may have exposed Social Security numbers of 4.9 million people
hero.body:
Unauthorized access to Florida’s student financial aid website may have exposed personal information, including Social Security numbers, belonging to approximately 4.9 million people, the Florida Department of Education said Thursday. Department staff became aware of the unauthorized access on Oct. 19. Officials believe the breach was limited to the Florida Student Financial Aid website.

The department recommends that people monitor their financial and online accounts for suspicious activity and regularly review account statements and credit reports. It also recommends considering a fraud alert or credit freeze with the major credit bureaus. Consumers can obtain free credit reports through AnnualCreditReport.com. The Federal Trade Commission’s IdentityTheft.gov website offers additional information about responding to a data breach.

Current financial aid is not at risk, and the incident will not delay financial aid disbursements or tuition payments from the department, officials said. The breach also will not affect eligibility for scholarships, grants or student loans from the department. Some department websites and online services may experience temporary disruptions while officials work to restore full functionality.

The department said it activated its cybersecurity response protocols after detecting the incident, took steps to contain the unauthorized activity and secure its systems, and notified the Florida Attorney General’s Office. It is working with the Florida Digital Service and the Florida Department of Law Enforcement. The unauthorized access remains under criminal investigation.

Anyone with questions about the breach can contact the department at databreach@fldoe.org. The department is posting updates on its data breach information page and said information could change as the criminal investigation continues.

hero.headline: State review finds St. Lucie County glioblastoma cases in line with expectations
hero.body:
An updated Florida Department of Health review of concerns about a possible glioblastoma cluster in St. Lucie County found 95 cases from 2019 through 2023, compared with 92 expected. Health officials say the difference is not statistically significant. The countywide analysis does not examine concentrations on particular streets or in specific neighborhoods, leaving families’ concerns about geographic patterns unresolved.

The findings largely match those of the state’s original 2019 report, which found that the number of cases did not warrant a more intensive investigation. Clint Sperber, administrator for the Florida Department of Health in St. Lucie County, said the latest review reached the same conclusion about expected cases. The review also considered existing water and radiation monitoring records. Unlike the 2019 report, the updated analysis did not break down cases by age or sex because officials said there were too few cases to make those comparisons statistically reliable.

Families’ concerns have centered partly on where patients lived. Some patients lived within blocks of one another, others on the same street. In one case, unrelated patients had lived in the same home. Area doctors and neurosurgeons also expressed concerns. Glioblastoma is most commonly diagnosed in older adults, but some of the local patients were in their 30s, and Kyle Vericella was 18. Sperber acknowledged that the updated analysis does not closely examine whether patients lived near one another on particular streets or within specific neighborhoods.

Deb Johnston wants investigators to look more closely at individual neighborhoods, particularly the White City area. Her son, Lenny Schelin Jr., died at 33, just 17 months after his glioblastoma diagnosis. Nearly eight years after his death, Johnston remains grateful that officials continue to review the cases, but she wants a closer examination of the geographic patterns. “I haven't given up; it's just you get tired,” she said.

The Florida Department of Health has invested at least $9 million in glioblastoma research since concerns about local cases drew attention. Johnston also supports research through an annual fishing tournament honoring her son, who loved fishing. The event has raised nearly $300,000 for glioblastoma research, and another tournament is approaching.
hero.article_text: Nearly eight years after WPTV first investigated concerns about a possible cluster of glioblastoma cases in St. Lucie County, health officials have reviewed the numbers again.The latest findings show the number of cases remains in line with what would be expected based on the county's population, but families who lost loved ones to the deadly brain cancer say important questions remain unanswered.WATCH THE REPORT BELOW: The latest review by the Florida Department of Health follows years of WPTV reporting into concerns raised by patients and families who discovered they lived near others diagnosed with the same aggressive form of brain cancer.While health officials say the data does not show a statistically significant increase in cases, the review does not examine whether patients were concentrated on particular streets or in specific neighborhoods.For families who have spent years searching for answers, that distinction matters.READ THE FULL STATE REPORT BELOW: A young man's death helped spark an investigationFor Deb Johnston, the loss of her son, Lenny Schelin Jr., is still painful."It's been eight years since Lenny passed," she said.Lenny was just 33 years old when he died from glioblastoma, one of the most aggressive forms of brain cancer.He was healthy, active and loved fishing. He survived just 17 months after his diagnosis."Everybody loved Lenny. He just had this charm about him," his mother recalled.Lenny's story was among the first that helped WPTV uncover concerns about glioblastoma cases in St. Lucie County.Other patients included Mark Cunningham, who was also in his 30s, and Kyle Vericella, who was just 18.After WPTV anchor Meghan McRoberts uncovered the local cases, dozens of additional patients and family members contacted her with their stories.Area doctors and neurosurgeons also expressed concerns.Glioblastoma is most commonly diagnosed in older adults, making the younger ages of some patients particularly troubling to their families.But it wasn't just their ages that raised questions.As patients began connecting with one another, WPTV mapped where they lived beginning in 2018.Some lived within blocks of one another. Others lived on the same street. In one case, unrelated patients had lived in the same home.The reporting drew attention from lawmakers, environmental advocate Erin Brockovich and the Florida Department of Health.What did the original 2019 investigation find?The concerns prompted health officials to examine glioblastoma cases in St. Lucie County."You brought it to my attention. It was alarming; it was nerve-wracking," Clint Sperber, administrator for the Florida Department of Health in St. Lucie County, told WPTV's Meghan McRoberts.Sperber said the concerns led to a request for assistance from Florida's cancer registry."I asked for assistance from our cancer registry through our leadership, my boss," he said. "And we were able to help collect a lot of information."That information was compiled into a report released in 2019.Despite concerns about the number of patients diagnosed with glioblastoma, the report did not find a statistically significant increase in cases that would warrant a more intensive investigation.Health officials also reviewed existing environmental monitoring information, including public water utility data and radiation monitoring records associated with the area's power plant.Sperber pointed to ongoing environmental monitoring as part of the state's assessment."There is water testing, there is vegetation testing, they look at watermelon, milk, fish, soil, they would know if there is any release of radiation," Sperber said.The findings were disappointing for families who had hoped the investigation would uncover an explanation."I was like deflated because we worked so hard," Johnston said.What does the latest glioblastoma review show?Seven years after the original report, health officials have taken another look at glioblastoma cases in St. Lucie County.Their conclusion remains largely unchanged."The conclusion that was found in 2019 is the same one we have today," Sperber told WPTV. "We are seeing the same ratio, the same expected number of cases that we would expect statewide for our county."According to Sperber, a county with approximately 400,000 residents would be expected to see about 14 to 15 new glioblastoma diagnoses each year.The report also shows that from 2019 to 2023, there were 95 cases of glioblastoma, just three cases more than the 92 expected.Health officials say the latest review does not identify an unusual increase in glioblastoma cases compared with statewide expectations.Unlike the 2019 report, however, the latest review does not break down cases by age or sex.Officials say there are too few cases to make those comparisons statistically reliable.The review also considered existing water and radiation monitoring records without identifying new concerns.What questions remain?Although the latest review did not find an unusual increase in glioblastoma cases countywide, it does not settle every question raised by patients and their families.Sperber acknowledged the analysis does not closely examine whether patients lived near one another on particular streets or within specific neighborhoods.That means the review's broader findings do not necessarily address the geographic patterns that originally concerned families, determining what causes glioblastoma is also challenging.Sperber pointed to recent research by the International Journal of Molecular Sciences identifying nearly a dozen potential factors associated with the disease, making it difficult to identify a single environmental source."I wish there was an answer," Sperber said. "I wish there was a smoking gun that says okay here is the reason, the cause, the source for glioblastoma."As St. Lucie County's population continues to grow, health officials expect the total number of diagnoses to rise as well.But for families who lost loved ones, the question remains whether the countywide numbers tell the entire story.A mother's call for a closer look at her hometownFor Johnston, hearing that the state's findings have not changed was difficult."I was deflated when you told me that. I was like, oh my God," she told McRoberts.She remains grateful that health officials are continuing to review the numbers.When asked whether she was glad the state was still looking into the issue, she responded, "Yes … it gives you hope for the others that come behind us."But she wants investigators to look more closely at individual neighborhoods, rather than relying on broader geographic data.When McRoberts asked where she would like additional testing conducted, her answer was immediate."In the White City area," she said.Nearly eight years after losing her son, Deb says the search for answers has taken an emotional toll."I haven't given up; it's just you get tired," she said.Millions invested in glioblastoma researchSince WPTV's initial reporting, the Florida Department of Health has invested at least $9 million in glioblastoma research.Deb has also worked to support research in her son's memory.Each year, she hosts a fishing tournament honoring Lenny, who loved spending time on the water.The event has raised nearly $300,000 for glioblastoma research.Another tournament is approaching, continuing her efforts to help other families facing the same devastating diagnosis.For Deb, the hope is that continued research and closer examination of local cases will eventually provide answers."I'm just glad you have followed through the way that you have," she told McRoberts.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. "And we were able to help collect a lot of information."That information was compiled into a report released in 2019.Despite concerns about the number of patients diagnosed with glioblastoma, the report did not find a statistically significant increase in cases that would warrant a more intensive investigation.Health officials also reviewed existing environmental monitoring information, including public water utility data and radiation monitoring records associated with the area's power plant.Sperber pointed to ongoing environmental monitoring as part of the state's assessment."There is water testing, there is vegetation testing, they look at watermelon, milk, fish, soil, they would know if there is any release of radiation," Sperber said.The findings were disappointing for families who had hoped the investigation would uncover an explanation."I was like deflated because we worked so hard," Johnston said.What does the latest glioblastoma review show?Seven years after the original report, health officials have taken another look at glioblastoma cases in St. Lucie County.Their conclusion remains largely unchanged."The conclusion that was found in 2019 is the same one we have today," Sperber told WPTV. "We are seeing the same ratio, the same expected number of cases that we would expect statewide for our county."According to Sperber, a county with approximately 400,000 residents would be expected to see about 14 to 15 new glioblastoma diagnoses each year.The report also shows from 2019 to 2023, there were 95 cases of glioblastoma, just three cases more than the 92 expected.Health officials say the latest review does not identify an unusual increase in glioblastoma cases compared with statewide expectations.Unlike the 2019 report, however, the latest review does not break down cases by age or sex.Officials say there are too few cases to make those comparisons statistically reliable.The review also considered existing water and radiation monitoring records without identifying new concerns.What questions remain?Although the latest review did not find an unusual increase in glioblastoma cases countywide, it does not settle every question raised by patients and their families.Sperber acknowledged the analysis does not closely examine whether patients lived near one another on particular streets or within specific neighborhoods.That means the review's broader findings do not necessarily address the geographic patterns that originally concerned families.Determining what causes glioblastoma is also challenging.Sperber pointed to recent research by the International Journal of Molecular Sciences identifying nearly a dozen potential factors associated with the disease, making it difficult to identify a single environmental source."I wish there was an answer," Sperber said. "I wish there was a smoking gun that says okay here is the reason, the cause, the source for glioblastoma."As St. Lucie County's population continues to grow, health officials expect the total number of diagnoses to rise as well.But for families who lost loved ones, the question remains whether the countywide numbers tell the entire story.A mother's call for a closer look at her hometownFor Johnston, hearing that the state's findings have not changed was difficult."I was deflated when you told me that. I was like, oh my God," she told McRoberts.She remains grateful that health officials are continuing to review the numbers.When asked whether she was glad the state was still looking into the issue, she responded, "Yes … it gives you hope for the others that come behind us."But she wants investigators to look more closely at individual neighborhoods, rather than relying on broader geographic data.When McRoberts asked where she would like additional testing conducted, her answer was immediate."In the White City area," she said. Nearly eight years after losing her son, Deb says the search for answers has taken an emotional toll."I haven't given up, it's just you get tired," she said. Millions invested in glioblastoma researchSince WPTV's initial reporting, the Florida Department of Health has invested at least $9 million in glioblastoma research.Deb has also worked to support research in her son's memory.Each year, she hosts a fishing tournament honoring Lenny, who loved spending time on the water.The event has raised nearly $300,000 for glioblastoma research.Another tournament is approaching, continuing her efforts to help other families facing the same devastating diagnosis.For Deb, the hope is that continued research and closer examination of local cases will eventually provide answers."I'm just glad you have followed through the way that you have," she told McRoberts.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. hero.headline: Erosion hits Ocean Drive beachfront parking in Vero Beach as king tides persist
hero.body:
Coastal erosion caused by king tides and strong onshore winds has affected a section of beachfront parking on Ocean Drive in Vero Beach, prompting officials to contact park officials about public safety measures. The area is one of the erosion hot spots officials have identified along the coast.

Quintin Bergman, the resource manager with Indian River County, is monitoring the damage along the Vero Beach boardwalk. He said the erosion is approaching severe as the two weather events continue to affect the shoreline. “I would classify this as leaning more on the severe side of erosion. It's not extreme by any means, but definitely we are very concerned,” Bergman said.

The forecast calls for elevated winds for a few more days, and king tides will continue to affect the water level, Bergman said. “We're still in the middle of this. We're not through with the weather event. The forecast is showing elevated winds for a few more days, and the king tide event is still going to be affecting the tide.” Officials plan to assess the damage after the weather event passes.

Beachgoers have also noticed changes to the shoreline. Svetlana Ryan was among those still enjoying the view in Vero Beach despite the erosion. “We noticed because there was so much sand before, and now it's just a wall. But you do with whatever you have to do here in Vero Beach,” Ryan said.

hero.headline: Murray Middle School breaks ground on $33 million rebuild after tornado damage
hero.body:
Murray Middle School has broken ground on a $33 million rebuilding phase that will add permanent learning and performing arts spaces after a tornado spawned by Hurricane Milton damaged three main buildings and forced students into portable classrooms. School officials expect gym renovations to be completed by August 2027 and the new buildings to be finished by December 2027.

Students and staff gathered for the groundbreaking as the school moves into the second phase of its campus rebuilding project. The work includes a performing arts wing with band and choir rooms, new learning spaces and gym renovations. Murray Middle School Principal Tiffany Roth said students will also have a new media center, an art room and an agriculture room.

Martin County Superintendent Michael Maine said campus improvements were planned before Hurricane Milton, but the storm damage added urgency. About $33 million has been approved for the second phase, according to school officials. “When Hurricane Milton came through and spawned the tornado, it took down three of our main buildings that we rely on every single day,” Maine said. “We couldn't have our students displaced in portables any longer than we needed to.”

Choir was among the programs forced out of permanent space by the storm. Dr. Anita Caswell, Murray Middle School's choir and drama director, said the damage destroyed decades of program materials, including costumes and props. “It was 60 years of drama props,” Caswell said. “Our dresses were in that, the boys' vest that we used to sing in, and just to see it all mangled and stuck up on the wall, it just hurt.”

Caswell said students continued singing in a portable classroom and earned straight superior ratings that year. Murray Middle student Nicholas Lowe said the move required him to adjust to a different learning environment. Roth said she hopes students take pride in being Murray Lions and enjoy the new buildings when they are finished.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County detective charged with DUI after Vero Beach crash, put on unpaid leave
hero.body:
St. Lucie County sheriff's detective Tyler Horstman has been charged with DUI and placed on unpaid administrative leave following a March 1 crash in Vero Beach that seriously injured a woman and hospitalized her son. Investigators said Horstman was off duty and driving an unmarked agency pickup truck when it collided with their SUV.

The crash happened at Beachland Boulevard and A1A. Investigators said the SUV's driver ran a red light while Horstman had a green light. All three people were hospitalized. The child was later released, but the woman suffered a traumatic brain injury, according to the affidavit.

Investigators determined that Horstman's blood alcohol level was above the legal limit. During his assessment, Horstman said he had consumed "a few beers" earlier in the evening, according to the affidavit. Police said the agency truck was traveling about 64 mph in a 35-mph zone just before the crash.

Horstman turned himself in to the Indian River County Jail on Monday. Police said the investigation took several months and involved search warrants, subpoenas and obtaining records. He faces several charges, including DUI. St. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro said Horstman was placed on unpaid administrative leave in accordance with agency policy.

"Our responsibility to uphold the law comes with an expectation that we follow it ourselves. When an employee is accused of violating that responsibility, we must address it fairly and hold them accountable through the appropriate process," Del Toro said in a statement.

hero.headline: Mattamy Homes transferring 125 acres in Martin County for St. Lucie River muck storage
hero.body:
Mattamy Homes is transferring 125 acres to Martin County to store muck dredged from the St. Lucie River as part of efforts to improve water quality. The removal project will begin once federal funding is authorized, a company official said.

The parcel is in the northern section of the Newfield development. The developer said the land was donated to the Comprehensive Everglades Restoration Plan, a federal plan to restore, protect and preserve South Florida's water resources.

James Fitzgerald, vice president of community development for Mattamy Homes Southeast Florida Division, said the Florida Inland Navigation District (FIND) is also donating an adjacent 125 acres. Together, the 250 acres can hold 2.4 million cubic yards of muck removed from the river, Fitzgerald said.

Fitzgerald said the muck will dry out after removal. He expressed hope that the land could eventually be used for recreation or, depending on the county's needs, other environmental restoration projects.

Fitzgerald said the Florida Inland Navigation District (FIND) is also donating an adjacent 125 acres. Combined, Fitzgerald said the 250 acres can hold 2.4 million cubic yards of muck from the river.WPTV asked Fitzgerald what happens to the muck after the removal project."The muck will dry out, and we're hoping at some point in the future that land can be used as a recreational project," Fitzgerald said. "Or perhaps, depending on the needs of the county, in some other future environmental restoration projects."Fitzgerald said the project to remove the muck will begin once federal funding is authorized.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce police seek missing endangered adult Joseph Lee Williams, 46
cards.teaser: Police say Williams requires medication and may be in emotional distress. He was reported missing Oct. 23 from the Prima Vista Boulevard area.
cards.body:
The Fort Pierce Police Department is asking for the public’s help finding Joseph Lee Williams, 46, whom authorities describe as a missing endangered adult. Police said Williams requires medication for health concerns and may be in emotional distress.

Williams was reported missing Oct. 23 from the Prima Vista Boulevard area, according to police. Investigators said he was last seen in Fort Pierce wearing a white T-shirt, black pants and shoes.

Anyone with information about Williams’ whereabouts is urged to contact the Fort Pierce Police Department at 772-979-1335. The investigation remains ongoing.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie man arrested, accused of trying to extort State Rep. Meg Weinberger
cards.teaser: Investigators say Anthony Pizzarelli demanded an apology and support for government audits, including in St. Lucie County. He denied using his communications as leverage.
cards.body:
A Port St. Lucie man was arrested on charges alleging he tried to extort State Rep. Meg Weinberger by threatening lawsuits and ethics complaints unless she publicly apologized and supported government audits, including in St. Lucie County. The allegations against Anthony Pizzarelli, 50, are outlined in a Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office probable cause affidavit.

Pizzarelli faces charges of extortion, using a two-way communication device to facilitate a felony, and harassing an elected official, according to the affidavit. He told investigators he viewed his communications as good faith notices and denied using them to leverage Weinberger. He said he wanted an apology over an incident involving an email on which she had been copied and was seeking her support for his complaints. He is presumed innocent unless proven guilty.

Investigators say Pizzarelli emailed Weinberger on Feb. 9, offering to leave her out of planned lawsuits and ethics complaints if she issued a swift public apology. He proposed wording for the apology. In an April 6 email, he allegedly renewed the threat and urged her to help with his audit campaign. According to the affidavit, he wanted audits of Palm Beach and St. Lucie counties and investigations into government contracting.

The affidavit says Pizzarelli sent a voice memo directly to Weinberger's personal cell phone on May 18, 2026. Among his statements were “I'm an angry person, so I'm not being nice,” and “you don't know what I can do.” Weinberger told investigators she viewed the messages as threats and feared for her safety and her family's safety. A first-term Republican, she represents Florida House District 94, which is entirely within Palm Beach County.

In 2025, Pizzarelli was arrested after being accused of sending threatening emails to St. Lucie County commissioners. Deputies said the communications escalated in tone and content, raising concern among officials. In the current affidavit, Pizzarelli told investigators that all charges from that case had been dropped.

Weinberger's campaign also faced a separate voter intimidation case during the 2024 election involving Nicholas Farley, not Pizzarelli. Farley was arrested after a campaign volunteer said he yelled antisemitic slurs at her and drove threateningly near early voters outside the Acreage Branch Library.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County deputy charged with DUI after Vero Beach crash, placed on unpaid leave
hero.body:
St. Lucie County sheriff's detective Tyler Horstman has been charged with DUI and placed on unpaid administrative leave following a March 1 crash in Vero Beach that seriously injured a woman and hospitalized her son. Horstman turned himself in to the Indian River County Jail on Monday.

Horstman was off duty and driving an unmarked agency pickup truck when it collided with an SUV carrying the woman and her son at Beachland Boulevard and A1A, investigators said. Investigators determined that the SUV's driver ran a red light and that Horstman had a green light. All three people involved in the crash were hospitalized. The child was later released, while the woman suffered a traumatic brain injury, according to the affidavit.

Investigators determined that Horstman's blood alcohol level was above the legal limit. According to the affidavit, he said during his assessment that he had “a few beers” earlier in the evening. Police also said the truck was traveling about 64 mph in a 35-mph zone just before the crash.

Police said the investigation took several months and involved search warrants, subpoenas and obtaining records. Horstman faces several charges, including DUI. His unpaid administrative leave follows agency policy, according to St. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro.

“Our responsibility to uphold the law comes with an expectation that we follow it ourselves. When an employee is accused of violating that responsibility, we must address it fairly and hold them accountable through the appropriate process,” Del Toro said in a statement. “The men and women of this agency work every day to earn the trust of our community, and we will continue to hold ourselves to the standards that trust requires.”

hero.headline: Murray Middle School breaks ground on $33 million rebuilding phase
hero.body:
Murray Middle School has broken ground on a $33 million rebuilding phase that will replace storm-damaged spaces and move displaced students and programs out of portable classrooms, according to Martin County school officials. The project follows damage to three main buildings from a tornado spawned by Hurricane Milton.

School officials said about $33 million has been approved for the second phase of the campus project. The work includes new learning spaces, a performing arts wing and renovations to the gym. The gym is expected to be completed by August 2027, with the new buildings expected to be finished by December 2027. Principal Tiffany Roth said the project includes a media center, an art room and an agriculture room, along with rooms for band and choir in the performing arts wing.

Students and staff gathered for the groundbreaking as rebuilding continued. Martin County Superintendent Michael Maine said improvements to Murray Middle School were planned before Hurricane Milton, but the tornado damage made the work more urgent. “When Hurricane Milton came through and spawned the tornado, it took down three of our main buildings that we rely on every single day,” Maine said. “We couldn't have our students displaced in portables any longer than we needed to.”

Choir was among the programs displaced by the storm. Dr. Anita Caswell, Murray Middle School's choir and drama director, said the storm destroyed decades of program materials, including costumes and drama props. “It was 60 years of drama props,” Caswell said. Her students continued singing in a portable classroom, and she said the choir earned straight superior ratings that year.

For student Nicholas Lowe, the move meant adjusting to a different learning environment. “It was a big change, but also I had to adapt to it to, like, be better for the choir,” Lowe said. Roth said she hopes the completed campus will give students a renewed sense of pride in being Murray Lions.

cards.headline: Siblings seek answers after St. Lucie County firefighter found unresponsive in bunk
cards.teaser: Austin Hodge’s siblings say the firefighter-paramedic appeared normal hours before he was found unresponsive at the firehouse. They are seeking answers about his death.
cards.body:
The siblings of St. Lucie County firefighter-paramedic Austin Hodge, who died on duty Oct. 24, say the 34-year-old was found unresponsive in his firehouse bunk early that morning. They are seeking answers about his final hours, and his family says they do not yet know what caused his death. His sister, Alexis Hodge, said relatives were told he had been cooking, talking on the phone and making jokes before going to bed. “Everybody that saw him said he was normal,” she said. Alexis and her brother, Javan Hodge, gathered at Austin’s home and remembered him as strong, fun, caring and dedicated to serving others. In addition to his work as a firefighter-paramedic, Austin worked as a respiratory therapist, his family said.

Javan said the family wants to understand the events leading to Austin’s death. “I want to know A to Z what happened,” he said. Alexis said relatives want to know who was around Austin and who saw him before he was found unresponsive. “After I get my answers, then I can rest and heal from my grief,” she said.

Austin’s death comes just over a year after the death of his 26-year-old brother, Jairus “Jay” Hodge, who also served with the fire district. The family said Jairus became sick while on shift in July 2025 and later died. Relatives raised concerns about the medical care Jairus received, and Austin sought answers and advocated for his brother. “He would not rest until he could get to the bottom of it,” Javan said.

Alexis and Javan said they intend to carry on both brothers’ legacy. Javan said Austin inspired him to pursue a career in healthcare. He is studying to become a nurse and preparing to graduate in December. “I do know I want to make him proud. I do know I want to make both of my brothers proud,” Javan said. “The love I have for them is unimaginable. It has no bounds.”

hero.headline: St. Lucie County detective charged with DUI, on unpaid leave after Vero Beach crash
hero.body:
St. Lucie County sheriff's detective Tyler Horstman faces charges including DUI and has been placed on unpaid administrative leave following a March 1 crash in Vero Beach that seriously injured a woman and hospitalized her son. Horstman, who was off duty at the time of the crash, turned himself in to the Indian River County Jail on Monday. His unpaid leave is in accordance with agency policy.

Police said Horstman's unmarked agency pickup truck was traveling about 64 mph in a 35-mph zone just before it collided with an SUV at Beachland Boulevard and A1A. Investigators said the SUV's driver ran a red light while Horstman had a green light. All three people involved were hospitalized. The child was later released, but the woman suffered a traumatic brain injury, according to the affidavit. Police said the crash could have been fatal.

Investigators determined that Horstman's blood alcohol level was above the legal limit. According to the affidavit, he said during his assessment that he had consumed “a few beers” earlier in the evening. Police said the investigation took several months and involved search warrants, subpoenas and obtaining records.

St. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro said the agency must hold employees accountable through the appropriate process when they are accused of violating the law. “Our responsibility to uphold the law comes with an expectation that we follow it ourselves. When an employee is accused of violating that responsibility, we must address it fairly and hold them accountable through the appropriate process,” Del Toro said.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County detective accused of speeding in Vero Beach DUI crash
hero.teaser: An arrest report says the woman in the other vehicle suffered a traumatic brain injury. The Sheriff’s Office has put its internal investigation on hold pending the criminal case.
hero.body:
St. Lucie County Detective Tyler Horstman is accused of driving 63 mph in a 35 mph zone before a March 1 crash in Vero Beach that left another driver with a traumatic brain injury. The allegations are detailed in an arrest report tied to the felony DUI case against Horstman, who turned himself in Monday afternoon after a warrant was issued.

The crash happened about 11:25 p.m. at Beachland Boulevard and A1A. According to the arrest report, Horstman was off duty and driving an unmarked St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office pickup truck when he struck a Chevy Equinox carrying a woman and an infant. Vero Beach police say Horstman entered the intersection on a green light and the other driver entered against a red light. Both drivers were injured and taken to the hospital. The report describes the woman’s injury as “a traumatic brain injury” and says the infant was alert and responsive.

The arrest report says Horstman acknowledged having a few beers earlier in the evening. It describes a “faint odor of alcohol on his breath” and says he was “lethargic and dazed” and “drowsy and periodically dozing off.” Blood-test results showed a blood alcohol concentration of 0.246, more than three times Florida’s legal limit, according to the Sheriff’s Office.

The Sheriff’s Office received those results September 9, and Horstman was placed on administrative leave September 15. The agency’s internal investigation is on hold pending the outcome of the criminal case. Vero Beach police are leading the criminal investigation.

The felony warrant issued Monday lists charges of DUI impairment involving a blood or breath alcohol level of 0.15 or higher and serious personal injury. Horstman was booked into the Indian River County Jail at 4:59 p.m. and posted $15,000 bond at 6:24 p.m. His arraignment is scheduled for December 9.

Vero Beach police say Horstman was driving at 63 mph in a posted 35 mph zone and entered the intersection on a green light. The other driver entered the intersection against a red light. It says Horstman had a "faint odor of alcohol on his breath" and it says Horstman was "lethargic and dazed" and that he was "drowsy and periodically dozing off." The woman in the vehicle he hit suffered "a traumatic brain injury" and the infant was alert and responsive. The arrest report says Horstman had a blood-alcohol level of .246, which is three times the legal limit at which a person is considered too impaired to drive in Florida. Horstman was placed on administrative leave on September 15, according to the St. A felony arrest warrant was issued Monday. It lists charges of DUI impairment involving a blood or breath alcohol level of 0.15 or higher and serious personal injury. The crash happened in March, but Horstman was not arrested until late October. "It's very typical in cases like this take months and months, and it's very frustrating for victims and their families, and also for the public, who are waiting for justice," said Dave Aronberg, former Palm Beach County State Attorney. He is now an attorney in private practice in West Palm Beach. Aronberg says it's not unusual at all that it would take seven months for someone, in this case a Sheriff's detective, to be arrested for DUI with serious bodily injury. "Proving felony DUI with serious bodily injury requires two hard sciences. You have to have crash physics to prove causation. That's crucial to any case like this, and you also have to have toxicology to prove impairment, and neither of those things happens overnight," Aronberg said. Horstman was booked into the Indian River County Jail at 4:59 p.m. and later posted $15,000 bond at 6:24 p.m. His arraignment is scheduled for December 9. cards.headline: Siblings seek answers after St. Lucie County firefighter Austin Hodge’s death
cards.teaser: Austin Hodge’s siblings say the family was told he was found unresponsive in his firehouse bunk. They are seeking answers about his final hours and what caused his death.
cards.body:
The siblings of St. Lucie County firefighter-paramedic Austin Hodge are seeking answers about his death after the 34-year-old died while on duty Oct. 24. His siblings, Alexis Hodge and Javan Hodge, want to understand what happened in his final hours and what caused his death.

Alexis said the family was told Austin appeared to be himself before going to bed. He had been cooking, talking on the phone and making jokes, according to the account relayed to them. “Everybody that saw him said he was normal,” she said. Alexis and Javan gathered at Austin’s home and remembered him as strong, fun, caring and dedicated to serving others. Along with his work as a firefighter-paramedic, Austin worked as a respiratory therapist, his family said.

Austin’s death came just over a year after the death of his younger brother, Jairus “Jay” Hodge, 26, who also served with the fire district. The family said Jairus became sick while on shift in July 2025 and later died. They raised concerns about the medical care Jairus received and said Austin sought answers and advocated for his brother. “He would not rest until he could get to the bottom of it,” Javan said. “He would not rest until he could spread Jay’s legacy globally.”

Now, Alexis and Javan are seeking answers about Austin. “I want to know A to Z what happened,” Javan said. Alexis said they want to establish who was around Austin and who saw him before he was found unresponsive. “After I get my answers, then I can rest and heal from my grief,” she said.

Both siblings said they are determined to make Austin and Jairus proud. Javan said Austin inspired him to pursue a career in healthcare. He is studying to become a nurse and preparing to graduate in December. “I do know I want to make him proud. I do know I want to make both of my brothers proud,” Javan said. “The love I have for them is unimaginable. It has no bounds.”

hero.headline: Kanner Highway data center exempt from Martin County's one-year application pause
hero.body:
The Florida Gateway Project, a proposed data center off Kanner Highway, remains exempt from the one-year pause on large-scale data center applications that Martin County commissioners unanimously approved at a second public hearing. County staff expect the proposal’s development review to take a year, even as the moratorium pauses other applications.

The Florida Gateway Project application was submitted Oct. 12, one day before commissioners held the first public hearing on the moratorium. The county attorney said the information arrived late the day before that hearing and that commissioners were alerted as soon as possible. Commissioner Blake Capps confirmed during the second hearing that the county had received a data center application on Kanner Highway. The proposal will proceed through the county’s development review process.

The moratorium gives staff time to study potential environmental impacts and establish rules for future projects. Every resident who spoke during public comment at the second hearing opposed the possibility of data centers in the county. Casey Darling, policy director for Friends of the Everglades, called for further study. "We simply do not have enough information on what we may be introducing to this ecologically sensitive region and the world's most extensive restoration effort. We need more study and the evaluation of potential impacts, especially in the 16-county greater Everglades region," Darling said.

A resident who said they live one mile from the proposed Florida Gateway Project raised concerns about its scale, electricity demand and potential water use. Resident Richard Miller also objected to locating data centers near people’s homes. "These things are not to be near people that are trying to conduct their ordinary lives," Miller said.
hero.article_text: Martin County commissioners unanimously voted during a second public hearing to implement a one-year moratorium on large-scale data center applications, giving staff time to study potential environmental impacts and establish rules for future projects. During the hearing, every resident who spoke during public comment opposed the possibility of data centers in the county. "We simply do not have enough information on what we may be introducing to this ecologically sensitive region and the world's most extensive restoration effort. We need more study and the evaluation of potential impacts, especially in the 16-county greater Everglades region," said Casey Darling, policy director for Friends of the Everglades. "I don’t want to spend another year or longer where somebody that I know is trying to do me great bodily harm. Folks, it’s in your hands. These things are not to be near people that are trying to conduct their ordinary lives," said resident Richard Miller. Commissioner Blake Capps confirmed there is an applicant for a data center. "One of them is the Florida Gateway Project, where this one project has been ... a data center application has come on Kanner Highway," Capps said. A resident who lives near the proposed site raised concerns about the scale of the project. "I happen to live one mile from this new proposed mega center, 100 MW, and 100 MW is like unbelievable to power 100,000 homes, and that's going to be a mile from me. Who knows how much water it's going to use," the resident said. Commissioner Vargas expressed frustration with the application process. "I was not too happy about hearing this application. I even requested the receipt, which I have here in my hand, and the date ... We should give them back and say they don't want you here. It's okay, you go elsewhere," Vargas said. The application for the Florida Gateway Project was submitted on Oct. 12, with the first public hearing held the following day. "We got the information late on the Monday before the 13th ... so, I didn't have the information in advance of the 13th. At the meeting on the 13th, I disclosed to everybody that I had just found out about it. I'm sorry, Commissioner, we did alert the commission as soon as we could," said County Attorney Elysse A. "I understand, but somebody took the money on this date is what I'm trying to say. Doesn't anybody talk to anybody here?" Vargas said. The application will go through the development review process, which staff said is expected to take a year. Aside from this application, there are currently no other large-scale data center applications pending. cards.headline: Family seeks answers in St. Lucie County firefighter Austin Hodge’s death
cards.teaser: Austin Hodge’s siblings say the 34-year-old was found unresponsive in his firehouse bunk after appearing normal hours earlier. They are seeking answers about his final hours.
cards.body:
The family of St. Lucie County firefighter-paramedic Austin Hodge, who died while on duty Oct. 24, says he was found unresponsive in his firehouse bunk early that morning and taken to a hospital. His siblings are seeking answers about his final hours and say they do not yet know what caused the 34-year-old’s death.

His sister, Alexis Hodge, said the family was told Austin had been cooking, talking on the phone and making jokes before going to bed. “Everybody that saw him said he was normal,” she said. Alexis and her brother, Javan Hodge, gathered at Austin’s home and remembered him as strong, fun, caring and dedicated to serving others. In addition to working as a firefighter-paramedic, Austin worked as a respiratory therapist, according to his family. “It’s a shock to literally all of us,” Alexis said. “Nobody knows what happened.”

Austin’s death came just over a year after the death of his younger brother, 26-year-old Jairus “Jay” Hodge, who also served with the fire district. The family said Jairus became sick while on shift in July 2025 and later died. They said concerns about the medical care Jairus received led Austin to seek answers and advocate for his brother. “He would not rest until he could get to the bottom of it,” Javan said. “He would not rest until he could spread Jay’s legacy globally.”

Now, Alexis and Javan want to understand what happened to Austin before he was found unresponsive, including who was around him and who saw him. “I want to know A to Z what happened,” Javan said. Alexis said getting answers is important to her grieving process. “After I get my answers, then I can rest and heal from my grief,” she said.

Both siblings said they are determined to make Austin and Jairus proud. Javan said Austin inspired him to pursue a healthcare career. He is studying to become a nurse and preparing to graduate in December. “I do know I want to make him proud. I do know I want to make both of my brothers proud,” Javan said.
